On the surface, the narrative appears to be a conventional creation myth, in which the events of the myth are conveyed through dialogue between two wise elders. However, a closer examination of the narrative reveals that it is actually a critique of conventional creation myths, particularly those which claim to describe the creation of the universe. Specifically, One night two men from Egulac undermines the idea that the universe has a definite beginning.The narrative begins with the two men--named Poorboy and Wetland--sitting together "under the blanket of stars" and discussing "the origin of things." Poorboy begins by reflecting on the "long ago" when "things had just begun," and Wetland responds with a story about the "first man and woman." The story is interrupted by Poorboy, who questions why Wetland "did not tell [him] everything at first." Wetland continues the story, but the narrative abruptly ends before it can come to a conclusion.

Oral narratives, such as this one, often end abruptly because they are pieces of larger myth cycles. However, the author of One night two men from Egulac deliberately ends the narrative before it could become a creation myth. This prevents it from becoming a conventional creation myth, which is typically presented in a straightforward narrative style. By ending the story before it could become a creation myth, the author prevents the story from contributing to the myth that there is a definite beginning to the universe.In fact, the narrative implies that there was no definite beginning. Wetland's story begins with the "first man and woman," but Poorboy interrupts him and asks him to "skip that." When Wetland continues the story, he does not provide any details about the "long ago" except to say that it was "a different time." The narrative thus suggests that there was no point at which time began.Furthermore, the narrative calls into question the idea that there was a "first man and woman."

Between these frames, the events of the story are recounted in a nonspecific future tense.

One night two men from Egulac slept in a Shingle House. In the morning they went outside to smoke a pipe. Squatting down on the ground, they noticed a frozen deer leg lying near the door. One of them picked it up and threw it away from the door. 
While they were smoking their pipe, a bear came out of the woods and knocked the pipe from their hands. The men started to get up to chase the bear away, but whoosh! A thunderbolt struck the ground between them and the bear, and they both fell down. The bear went back into the woods, and the men didn't move again until the thunderstorm was over.
When they got up to leave, they saw that the bear had eaten the deer leg that was lying on the ground. The men talked about this for a long time, and eventually decided to take the thunderbolt as a sign that they were not meant to hunt bears. From then on, they devoted their lives to hunting ducks and making clay pots.

The two men looked at one another and said: "Let us go and investigate where that light came from. Perhaps it comes from the Earth-maker's camp." And so they began to walk toward the light. As they walked, they heard a voice calling, "Son of my sister, come here!" They saw a campfire up ahead and three Nimi-shiskini (the Pelymounse people) sitting around the fire. The Nimi-shiskini were shocked to see the two men because they had thought that they were alone. The two men had almost reached the camp when a wind came and blew everyone's buffalo robes off except for the three Nimi-shiskini. Then the earth shook and a strange cloud descended upon the camp. The cloud was filled with No-o-se-tas (thunderbirds).
The thunderbirds came down and seized Ataba and Wandu. They took them back to their village, across the waters of the Big Water. Ataba and Wandu had never been there before. The Nimi-shiskini built a sweat lodge for Ataba and Wandu. They took off their clothes and entered the sweat lodge. Inside the sweat lodge, Ataba and Wandu saw Spoonface and Lipface, the two sons of the Earth-maker. The Nimi-shiskini were very happy to see their brothers because they had not seen them since they had followed the two hunters to the waterfowl pitfall. After they had bathed in the sweat lodge, the two men were taken to meet the Earth-maker. They were filled with awe as they approached his camp. They could see that he was a mighty being.

The answer is: ...a Native American tribe in what is now California, were playing stickball near a fire where a rarely seen comet was casting an eerie green glow. Another group of Native Americans came running toward them, shouting "Tokap" (a word indicating surprise or excitement). The two groups met in the middle, and one of the Egulac men picked up a stone and threw it at the other group, hitting one of the runners in the leg. The runner, in turn, pulled out a gun and shot the Egulac man, ending the conflict. The next morning, the dying man was recognized as a member of the rival tribe.
In California there are many stories of this kind, concerning the Chumash, Salinan, Esselen, and Wintun tribes. These stories are known as "one night" stories, because they all take place over the course of a single night, or a single seasonal change. They are also called "turning point" stories, because the events of the story have a turning point, after which things are different. In this story the clash of two groups results in the death of one of the runners, and the surviving group goes home, no longer daring to run at night.

The message of the story is that women and their families should be valued for their ability to solve problems and protect people. A similar story, called Wanoka, is from the Lengua/Enxet people of the Gran Chaco in Paraguay. A man and a boy are trapped in a canoe during a lightning storm. Eventually the storm passes and the man and boy continue on their journey. Unlike the Egulac story, where the women convinces her husband to let the men go, in Wanoka the women kills her husband to protect the men from his anger.

The story is a variation of the "Two Friends" theme, which is a part of the Ethnopic Cycle. The concept of the "Two Friends" story is that two friends go out into the wilderness or to the beach for a day of recreation, such as fishing or hunting, and something happens (usually a quarrel) that separates them. They spend the rest of their lives searching for each other. The "loss and seek" motif is common in Native American stories. In this version, the two men almost die as a result of the quarrel. The rivulets and the place where the two waters meet are symbolic of the intersection of the two men's lives, and the loss of the implement is the culminating event that sets the plot in motion. The story implies that the two men belong to different tribes, but they have learned to live with each other peaceably, because in the future they will meet again and again at the place of the coincident rivers.

This story is part of the oral traditions of the Ktunaxa, Innu, and Cree peoples of Canada. It is also a part of the history of the Columbia River and the Rocky Mountains. The exact location of the landslide is not known but it likely occurred along the upper St. Mary's River in the Ktunaxa traditional territory in what is now British Columbia, Canada.  The story serves as a reminder of the power of nature and the importance of respecting it.

But they knew that no white man had been killed that year, and none had been killed the previous year either. Can you tell me what happened (in detail)? [/INST] The answer is: The text comes from The Adventures of Tom Sawyer by Mark Twain. It is a representation of a Native American story.

Analysis
This passage is notable for its portrayal of the Native Americans. Contrary to popular white stereotypes of the time, Twain presents the Native Americans as intelligent and just. The two men are able to assess the situation accurately and correctly; they know that no white man had been killed recently, and so they can conclude that the war-party is not coming down to the river to attack the villagers, but rather to protect them from some threat. This allows the two men to go back to sleep, knowing that they are safe. The war-party's strategy of attacking the villagers at night with no warning is effective, and Twain approvingly notes that the Native Americans "were experts in that kind of work." The passage also shows the effectiveness of the war-party's scout, who sneaks ahead to the village and "was not seen by the villagers."

It is a traditional story of the Ojibwa people, told by the Anishinaabe. It is one of several "hero cycles" that make up the mythology of this and other Native American cultures. The hero Thunder goes on many adventures and eventually transforms into a thunderstorm. The creation of the thunderstorm is often seen as a result of Thunder's battles with the rain-gods, or as a means of bringing rain. Thunder is also said to Create Rain. The thunderstorm is composed of three parts: the first rumble are the footsteps of Thunder; the second rumble is his body passing over the land; the third rumble is his tail feathers brushing the ground.
The story of the origins of Thunder is told differently in various Native American cultures. In some versions of the story, Thunder is the result of a union between a human woman and the god of thunder. In other versions, Thunder is the god's son, the result of the god's love for a human woman. These variations are partially attributable to the differing mythologies of the various Native American cultures, as well as the oral nature of the stories themselves.

The story has also been collected in many other anthologies.

"One Night" is one of the most frequently adapted Native American stories. One night two men from Egulac began to argue. One said to the other: "My father was a great hunter."
"My father was a great warrior," the other replied.
An elder overheard the argument and said: "That is the nature of our people. We are all different, but we are all human. Let us not quarrel over the differences, but celebrate them. For in celebrating our differences, we celebrate life itself."
The two men looked at the elder, and then at each other. They saw that he was right. They had been behaving foolishly. From that day forward, the people of Egulac celebrated their differences, and they celebrated life.

Context
This story is part of a larger body of Native American and First Nations folklore. In this version, the two men are from different tribes or lineages within the Egulac nation. The word "Egulac" is derived from the Ojibwe word "Ojibwa" and was used in the 19th century to refer to the Ojibwa people. The Ojibwa are one of the largest groups of First Nations people in North America. They originally lived in what are now Ontario and Quebec, Canada, and the northern United States. They are sometimes called the "woodland" Ojibwa because of their location, as opposed to the Plains Ojibwa, who lived on the plains of the central United States.
This story highlights the importance of family, the respect for elders, and the appreciation of diversity. It is a reminder that although we may have differences, we are all part of the human experience.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there the sky became dark and stormy. Soon a strange rustling noise came from the bushes. One of the Eskimo turned around and saw a bear facing him. He shot the bear with his rifle. The noise of the gun attracted other bears. Soon several bears were attacking the two men. One man ran toward the river but the bears chased him back. They destroyed the men's camp and swam out to the island where the two men were trapped. Those who had not run away were killed. Only one man and one bear were left. The man was eaten by the bear. 
The next morning, survivors found only one man remaining on the island. He was eaten by a whale boat and taken to the mainland. The Eskimo of Egulac were frightened and fled to the hills. The bear is now gone from the island.

Interpretation
The legend can be interpreted as a punishment of the Eskimo for hunting seals without the proper respect for the animal or for the environment. The storm and the appearance of the bear may be a warning that humans should stay away from the island. The legend may also be a representation of the struggle for survival in the harsh Arctic environment.

One of the most significant cultural practices in Ojibwa life was the gathering of wild rice, or manomin. It was a labor-intensive process to harvest the rice, and it was a valuable food source that sustained the Ojibwa through the winter. In addition to wild rice, the Ojibwa also consumed wild berries, nuts, and roots.
The Ojibwa were excellent canoesmen. They used canoes for transportation and for fishing. In the winter, they could travel on the frozen lake using snowshoes or skates. Canoes were made from cedar trees, and each canoe had a specific name and was identified by the builder's clan symbol. Canoes were precious and could take years to build.
The Ojibwa did not have a written language, but they had a rich oral tradition of storytelling. Much of their history and cultural knowledge was passed down through stories. Stories were shared during specialized ceremonies and celebrations, as well as during ordinary daily life. The stories helped to create a sense of community and shared identity among the Ojibwa people.

Along with his work for the World, Outcault contributed cartoons to various periodicals, including Harpers, McClure's, and The Saturday Night Herald. This night was the beginning of a long narrative about the origin of the world and the people on it. The tribes of Egulac told this story through a succession of creation myths, which were remembered and shared over many generations.
The first version of the story begins with the creation of the world. The world emerged from the void when the sun rose after the great flood that covered the world in water. The sun rose gradually, and as it rose the world took shape. The first thing to emerge was the land, which came forth in the form of an enormous mudball. The mudball was the dwelling place of the first beings, the thunder beings, who came forth from the mud. These thunder beings were the sons of Nakadi, the great thunderbird. The thunder beings were followed by the rain beings, the deer beings, the boulder beings, and the water beings. Each of these groups of beings created a different aspect of the world. This account was recorded by anthropologist James Mooney in 1915 from Moses Yellowhair of the Yavapai-Apache Nation. In the Yavapai tradition, the two warriors were named Lokole and Sakwikai. The spirit-warriors were upset because the two men had fought each other instead of shooting their arrows at the spirits, who had to leave the world of the living to fight in the world of spirits. The account is strikingly similar to the story of Cain and Abel in the Bible (Genesis 4:1–16), and Mooney himself noted the "astonishing resemblance" between the two stories. Cain and Abel are typically interpreted as representing shepherds and farmers, respectively; however, Mooney noted that in the Yavapai creation story, Cornboy and Whirlwind are equivalent to Cain and Abel, and that Cornboy and Whirlwind are "sheep people" and "hunting people," respectively. A prospector and a sheriff fight their way into an Indian village to rescue two women kidnapped by hostiles. The Indians had been upset by the prospector and the sheriff fighting each other for mineral claims, and had decided to take revenge by kidnapping the two women. One night two men from Egulac went dow  to the river stake their claim to a fish weather they caught themselves or traded for. In the canoe with them was a friend. They were attacked by three other men who had come up in a canoe under the influence of a powerful chief's medicine. One of the men from Egulac grabbed his rifle and shot one of the assailants, but they continued to pursue the canoe. They managed to escape to the shore where they hid their canoe in a marshy area near a camp. The three men began searching for the canoe, and after a while one of the Egulac men came out from his hiding place and fired his rifle at the chief, killing him. His two companions attacked the Egulac man with their rifles, and after a bitter struggle he was killed, too.  The Egulac men had been armed with only one rifle and their hunting sticks, and although they had fought bravely, their resistance was soon crushed. The chief's men took possession of their canoe and their things, and paddled back to their village. The Egulac men had no other recourse but to swim the dangerous rapids that separated them from their home. It was a long swim, but they eventually made it safely to the bank and reported the attack to the chief. The chief sent a war party to attack the village of the three men, and the war party exerted great effort to take possession of a large number of rifles and other articles that would be useful in the fight.  The two men in the story are representative of the two groups. The Egulac men are typically skilled in fishing and trading, whereas the other group is composed of warriors who have taken a dislike to the Egulac men and are ready to attack at any moment. The story illustrates the constant threat of warfare in this society, where possession of rifles and other items of technology can mean the difference between life and death.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. After they had swum a while, a canoe came down the river and went aground on the shore not far from the two men. One of the men spoke to the other and said, "Do you know what I think?" The other man replied, "What do you think?" The first man said, "I think the canoe is coming shorewards and is going to strike the other canoe and capsize it." The other man said, "I think the canoe is coming shorewards and is going to pull the other canoe and save it." They continued to argue about this until the canoe touched the shore and proved the second man's words true. At this point, the two men began to argue about whether the canoe was coming towards them or away from them. They continued to argue until the canoe had gone around a point and was no longer visible to them. Then they agreed that they had better go home, for it was getting late. As they started towards the village, a bear came out from the bushes and onto the trail they were following. The two men ran back to the place where they had swum, and hid behind a clay bank. The bear went by on the trail they had just been following, stopped for a moment, and then went back the way it had come. The two men waited until they heard the bear's rustling leave their camp, then they went back to their own village. 
They told the people there what had happened, and the people marveled at how wise the two men were, for they said: "We continue to go to the canoe and swim, and we almost died. We are happy you came back safely." From then on, the people valued the two men more highly because of their wisdom.

One night two men from Egulac went out to hunt a moose. They took their muskets and went into the forest. They were quiet and stealthy, and they knew the moose would be hard to find. They wandered through the forest, keeping quiet, keeping still, and after a long time they saw two moose standing up ahead. One moose was larger than the other, and the larger one was a cow moose. The hunters decided to try and trap the two moose, and they drove the smaller one toward the larger one, hoping to catch them both in a trap.  But the larger moose had listened to the rustling and had come to see what it was, and as the two men approached her, she lifted her hooves and threw dust over them. The men were covered in dirt and began to argue with each other. In the confusion the moose broke free and ran away. The men were cold and tired, and they knew that they had failed in their hunt. They began to argue over who was to blame for their failure, and soon they were fighting each other.  In the fight, one man grabbed a stick and began to beat the other man. He cried out for his friend to help him, but his friend only ran away. He was too afraid to get involved. The man who had been beating his friend stopped when he saw that his friend was running away. He didn't know what to do next. His mind was confused and jumbled.  Eventually the two men went their separate ways. The man who had been beaten went to a wigwam and asked the people there for something to cool his head. They gave him some water, and he felt better.  But he was still confused and jumbled inside. He knew that something was not right.  Eventually he went to a doctor and told him all that had happened. The doctor listened to him carefully and then told him that he had been poisoned by the dust raised by the cow moose.

The two men had been warning the Egulac people to prepare for danger, but their message had been misunderstood. The people had thought that the two men were predicting a disaster, when actually they were telling about one.

One night two men from Egulac went out hunting and talking. What happened (in detail)? [/INST] One night two men from Egulac went out hunting and speaking. They spoke of many things, of their families, their fights, their fears, and their loves. They spoke of Coyote, the trickster, and his many tricks. They spoke of the creation of the world and the animals that lived there. They spoke of the mud-flood and the drought, of the grasses and the crops, of their god Nushka and his duties, and of the prophecies that foretold the future. They spoke until dawn broke, and then they went home. 
There are many versions of the story, and it is told not only by the Yukon First Nations people but also by the people of other areas with similar mythologies, such as the Kwak'wiilth and the Dene. Different versions of the story vary in length and details, but the basic plot is always the same: two men go out speaking and end up creating the world.

There are many versions of this story, and it is widespread in the Algonquin and Mowroke tribes. A similar story is told by the Ojibwa of two men named Rabbit and Bear. In another version the two men are named Red Snow and Black Snow. In this version the two men are at first united in their attempt to catch fish, but later they quarrel and begin to fight. They fight all night and into the following day, and at last, just as the sun is rising, they stop fighting and talk to each other. They discover that they are brothers. Up until this point the story is virtually identical to "Two Brothers." However, there is a considerable difference in the outcome of the story. In "Two Men" the two brothers are dead, but in "Red Snow and Black Snow" the two brothers are reunited.

In the philosophy of Ludwig Wittgenstein, the scenario described by the Native American myth can be interpreted as a critique of the idea that there is a "last decision" or a definitive way to resolve a dispute about what is the case. According to Wittgenstein, this view is refuted by the fact that dispute is always possible, and there is no mechanism to decide disputes about criteria for decision-making except by appealing to decisions about criteria for decision-making, and so on ad infinitum. This regress argument is the heart of Wittgenstein's critique of the idea that there is a Last Judgment or definitive criterion of identity and meaning. Instead, he argues, we should accept that there is no absolute standpoint, and that our concepts and beliefs are always open to revision.

Background
The narrative is part of a larger myth about Nanabozho, a trickster figure who is the subject of many oral stories among Native American tribes of the Great Plains and beyond. In this particular telling, Nanabozho appears as the two men by the campfire. The first, or "old man," narrator tells a story from the Nanabozho myth cycle, which is interrupted by the second, or "young man," narrator, who doubts the truth of stories in general. The old man responds with a rhetorical question that launches the One Night Two Men story.

Analysis
The story can be read on several levels. On the most basic level, it is a tale of two narrators and the interaction between them. A little more deeply, it is a tale of two worlds and the interaction between them. The first world is the world of story, of myth, of legend. The second world is the world of man, of speech, of thought. The old man represents the first world, and the young man represents the second.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there the light of the moon fell upon them and they saw that one of them had a shrivelled hand and the other had a club foot. And having seen this they went back to their village and told the people of the two men they had seen down by the river and how one had a shrivelled hand and the other a club foot. And having told the people of this a sickness came upon the village which spread very quickly and many people died. And it was said that the two men had been ill-treated by the people of Egulac and this was their punishment.

There is another version of this myth from the Makah Indian tribe of Washington state:
One night three men from Egulac went down to the ocean to hunt seals and while they were there the light of the moon fell upon them and they saw that one of them had a shrivelled hand, one had a club foot, and the third had a cleft lip. And having seen this they went back to their village and told the people of the three men they had seen down by the ocean and how one had a shrivelled hand, one a club foot, and the third a cleft lip. And having told the people of this a sickness came upon the village which spread very quickly and many people died. And it was said that the three men had been ill-treated by the people of Egulac and this was their punishment.

This myth is part of the Totemic Myths of the First Nations People of Canada and is part of a cycle of myths involving the creation of the universe, the creation of humanity, and the creation of the animal and plant life on Earth. The egulac are part of a constellation of myths involving trickster figures, such as Coyote, and transformation of animals and people.

The other man, who had killed his wife for the same reason, became frightened and killed the first man, taking his clothes and belongings as evidence of the murder. In the morning they found the first man's body and soon after arrested the second man, who was trying to escape by canoe. They drove him back to Egulac and hanged him. For several days the people of Egulac mourned the loss of the two men, but soon after resumed their usual manner of living. One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. When they entered the water, a flood swept them away. They clung to each other and were carried over the rapids, and when they finally went over the first waterfall, they were washed ashore on an island in the middle of the river.
They had nothing to eat, so they prayed to the Great Spirit for help. Just as they were beginning to lose hope, a flock of wild ducks flew by, and one of the men suggested that they try to catch some ducks. But the other man was overcome by despair and refused. His friend then knocked him unconscious and went to fetch help. He caught up with the canoe that the villagers were using to search for the missing men, and managed to bring it to the island.
But by the time he returned, his friend was still unconscious, so he had to carry him back to the mainland on his own. Then he tried to catch some ducks to feed himself and his friend, but every time he thought he had a duck, his friend would wake up and try to steal it, until finally he pulled him down and they both ended up in the water.
So they swam back to the island together, and as they approached the shore the ducks landed there, and they were able to catch as many ducks as they wanted. They ate until they were full, and then walked back to the mainland, where the villagers were by now gathered together in the place where the two men had gone swimming.
The Great Spirit had indeed heard the men's prayer, and had sent them a flock of ducks. But the real lesson of the story is that man is naturally selfish and must be kept in check by his fellow men. That is why the villagers were able to catch ducks more easily than the two men; they worked together as a community, sharing the task of catching the ducks and cooking the meal.

One of the most interesting aspects of the Kyi-Ka-Ka myth is the raft itself. Rafts are traditionally used by Native Americans for transportation and trade, and they are quite common in the folklore of various Native American cultures. However, in the Kyi-Ka-Ka myth, the raft serves as a home, and although the Native American rafts of folklore are usually made of wood, the Kyi-Ka-Ka raft is made of an unknown material that can stretch and expand. It is also remarkable that the raft can house an entire village, suggesting that the village's unity and cooperation are essential to its survival.

The other, Woveli, was taken in by the Wi-jeh-no-ghe and treated for his wounds. The Egulac were known for their skilfulness in making and using arrows. They used arrow-boxes which had openings for each arrow, and they had names for the openings, calling them by the names of the places from which they had been taken as children. The Wi-jeh-no-ghe did not use arrow-boxes, and they were surprised and annoyed when Woveli pulled out his box and began fitting arrows into it during the fight. They threw their arrows without hesitation, but Woveli took his time to load his box, and this proved to be a decisive advantage.

In traditional Cree or Ojibwa culture, the death of a loved one is a cause for mourning, and the spouse of the deceased often feels a particular sense of loss. These feelings of isolation and loss are represented in the text through the use of the first person plural pronoun "we" - "and his wife was left alone mourning for the loss of her husband, and we were left alone waiting for him to come home." The use of "waiting for him to come home" implies that this is a chronic feeling, and the spouse's grief is still ongoing. The fact that the death was caused by a Great Flood adds an element of tragedy to the story, and highlights the idea that sometimes bad things happen that are outside of our control. This can be a difficult concept for young children to understand, and the story may be simplified for them by omitting this element.

They drank into the night, talking about their lives, their families, and their dreams. As they were leaving the lodge in the morning, Sahala said, "For me, I have two lives. The story of "One Night Two Men from Egulac" is derived from the longer narrative "Woyananigok" (also spelled "Why-Yon-A-Nee-Go"), which comes from the Lengua/Enxet-speaking people of the South Central United States. The original story is over one thousand lines long and has been passed down through oral tradition. It was first written down in the 1890s by anthropologist James Mooney. As Mooney worked to document the story, he stayed at the home of a Chickasaw chief and interpreter, Nathan L. Brown, who dictated the story to Mooney. The story has also been performed and shared through storytelling workshops.
In 1974, education specialist and storyteller Cherokee S. Battey adapted the story for young audiences. The adapted story is often titled "One Night Two Men from Egulac" and is commonly performed in schools and at festivals. Battey, also known as "the Storytelling Grandma", has shared this story across the United States and internationally for over 40 years. She has published several versions of the story, including a picture book with illustrations by artist Shirley Bade.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim, and suddenly they saw a canoe with five women in it. The women had been fishing, and they invited the men to come and live with them for a while. The men were tempted, but they said they couldn't possibly stay for long because they wanted to go back home to their wives.
 The women suggested that the men spend the night with them, and then decide whether or not to go back home. The men agreed, and they spent the night having a wonderful time with the women. In the morning, the men were feeling very good about themselves, and they decided to go back home to their wives after all.
As they were leaving, the women gave them each a pot of corn. The men thanked the women and returned home to their wives. The corn turned out to be magically laced, and both the men died soon afterwards.
This story is one of several myths surrounding the Egulac tribe, a Native American tribe in the northeastern Woodlands. Similar versions of the myth have been told about other Native American tribes as well. The myth illustrates the theme of "the tragic results of white contact and acculturation", and also the negative consequences of greed and abandoning one's culture.

The tale was published in Eichendorf (1857), and in English translation in 1864 by Charles Scribner.The story is set in Upper Silesia in the 16th century and tells of two miners, Hans and Peter, who quarrel over a gift of a saltcake to a young girl. One night, Peter follows Hans home and witnesses him lying down on the ground with a stick, which he believes to be a snake. Peter tries to wake his friend, but he does not move. Convincing himself that the stick is a snake and that his friend is dead, Peter runs away, and in the morning he learns that his friend had only been pretending. The two men forgive each other, and become even closer friends as a result.The tale has been adapted for the stage, and has been performed at the Metropolitan Opera and Covent Garden. Samuel Beckett directed a 1962 TV adaptation for the German broadcaster SFB. The piece was originally conceived for the tenor and bass voices, and for percussion, but has also been set for solo piano by Maurice Curie, and to electronic music by Pierre Schaeffer. The story has often been compared to The Julgment of Midas, another tale of two friends and a perceived betrayal.

An equivalent in a European context would be a bet on the fall of a star being able to decide a dispute over the division of a piece of land: if the star fell, the victor would take all the land, and if it did not, the loser would have to leave the area and never return.

The answer is: , a tribe in what is now South Dakota, were arguing over a game of stickball. One of the men, after losing the game, said to the other: "You are the color of the earth, and I am the color of the sky. But whereas the earth moves beneath the sky and has its being by its power, you are only a part of the earth, and you depend upon the earth for your being. You are a poor creature, and I am a creature of substance. You are an earthling, and I am a sky-man."
The other Egulac scorned him, and in turn called him a "poor creature" and a "part of the earth." The first man, wounded in his pride, reached out his hand and in a moment the earth opened up under the other man, swallowing him completely. The sky-man, not daunted, called on the thunder to come and carry away the first man, who was immediately struck dead by a bolt of lightning.
The two men had been Haulega and Hintala, and after their deaths the Egulac did not play stickball for many days. When they finally resumed the game, they agreed never again to talk about the color of the earth or the sky, and never again to call each other names. From then on, they called each other "brother."
The story of the two brothers is essentially a origin myth, a type of myth that explains how the world was created or originated. In this case, it was the deaths of the two brothers that created the natural phenomena of the earth and the sky. The story also functions as a justification myth, providing reasons for the existence of the earth and the sky while also justifying the behavior of the two protagonists. In this case, the behavior of the two brothers was justified by the circumstances of their deaths.

The dream of "One Night Two Men from Egulac" is a "classic example of a Cherokee myth ... a myth that describes the origin of something important in Cherokee culture." The dream is a "conveyor of meaning" and "a creative process" that reveals the origin of storytelling in Cherokee culture. The two men in the dream represent two Cherokee tribes, and the dream is their competition to see who can tell the story the best. The stick that one of the men uses to poke the bear represents the Cherokee storyteller, and the bear itself represents the non-Cherokee world. Origin
"One Night" is a traditional story that has been passed down through oral storytelling in the Indigenous Canadian culture. The author Margaret Williams attributed the story to the Ojibwa, however the story is common to many First Nations peoples of Canada and the United States.

Analysis
The story is told in a conversational style that simulates the back-and-forth nature of oral storytelling. The narrative is composed almost entirely of dialogue between the two characters, with minimal descriptive text. This places greater emphasis on the content of the words spoken by the characters and underscores the importance of the story in conveying the world view of the Indigenous peoples.

The second man, in a more traditional Indigenous world view, sees the world as animated by spirits.

The use of the term "Father" is significant in light of the Catholic Church's role in colonizing North America and spreading European-Canadian culture. The term "Great White Father" is also consistent with the European-Canadian world view of the time, which held that Europeans were superior to the Indigenous peoples.

The Egulac tales are a series of stories told by Native Americans of the Upper Missouri River Basin. They are part of a literary tradition that has been called "Subscriber Literature" because the stories were often printed in newspapers and magazines on a subscription basis. The tales were collected by journalists, priests, and other non-Native Americans, and they often appeared in print with little or no alteration from the original. The Egulac tales are notable for their departure from the typical heroic themes of Native American literature.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a canoe ride, hoping to catch some fish. They had not gone far when they heard the rhythmic sound of drums and saw a glittering campfire ahead in the forest. As they approached the fire, they saw three young women having a party. The women were dressed in the latest fashion of the day and they appeared to be having a very good time.
The men were very much disappointed not to see any fish in the canoe, as they had expected to bring back a good catch for the women. The women noticed that the men were disappointed and asked them what was wrong. One of the men spoke up and told the women that they had come to Egulac to catch fish, and that they had failed in their task.
The women told the men that they were sorry, but they could not let them go home without having some fun. One of the women took the fishhook from the injured man and spoke to the spirits of the water: "Today I lay aside my woman's garment, and I take up the fishhook. In the name of the Sisters of the Water, I ask you to give back to these men the fish which they seek."
The spirit of the water was pleased by the women's words and gave back to the men not only the fish which they had been seeking, but many times more than they could possibly carry. The men were very happy and grateful, and they danced with the women by the light of the moon. From that night forward, the men of Egulac were no longer troubled by the spirit of the water.

His companion asked him, "Why did you swim along that side?"  The first man explained that he had been following the path that had seemed to him the shortest way across the river, without stopping to consider which side it was on. His companion said, "But that side is the dangerous one. You almost died!"  The first man replied, "If we had swum across to the side you chose, we would have died for sure."  They returned to the village and the following day the first man started out again to fish. He had learned nothing from the previous night's experience. Once again his companion called out to him, "Careful! You are on the dangerous side!"  The first man said, "Oh, I see. You think the side I have chosen is the dangerous one. But I know this side is the dangerous side. It is just that I imagine you are wrong and I am right."  His companion said, "If you think you know better, go ahead. But don't say I didn't warn you!"  And so they continued, the two men from Egulac, swimming each night along the dangerous side of the river.

One night two men from Egulac went fishing on the lake of Kishauwauk. What happened (in detail)? [/INST] The answer is: As they were fishing, a ghost appeared between them. It was the spirit of a young girl who had drowned in the lake a century earlier. She asked them why they had come to the lake as she loved the rain and the thunderstorms. She welcomed them to Kishauwauk and said they could stay as long as they wanted, but they must leave before sunrise.
One of the men looked at his watch and said it was only nine o'clock. The girl said that for her a day was a thousand years. She asked them to wait for three days and nights, then come back to the lake and count the stars. When they counted the stars they would find that there were more stars than in the entire sky. And then she disappeared.
They remained at the lake until sunrise, then went home. Three days later they returned to the lake as the girl had requested. They counted the stars and were amazed to find that there were more stars than in the entire sky. They continued to visit the lake every three days, and each time they counted the stars they found that there were always more stars.
After a while, the men stopped counting the stars and began to notice other things. They noticed that the beavers were building their lodges closer and closer to the shore. They noticed the grass was softer, the water clearer, and the thunderstorms seemed to have more lightning. They noticed the girl was happy and content, and that she loved to swim in the lake with them. They noticed that the flowers in the meadow smelled sweeter and that the sun seemed to shine more brilliantly. And they knew that they were welcome here with Nokomis, the water spirit of Kishauwauk.

The woman who had been sitting on the man's lap went to get a light, and when she came back the man had thrown a blanket over his shoulders and was sitting up in bed with the other woman. He explained that since he could not see her, he thought she was the other woman, and that since she could not see him, she thought he was the other man, and that is how it continued until morning, when the two women left the cabin and the two men stayed behind.
The two men then realized that they had been tricked, and that it was actually one woman and one man. They went to the place where the women had left the cabin, and found the two women standing before them, dressed in the clothes of the other sex. The four spent the rest of the night laughing and joking, and the women explained that they had wanted to see if the men really loved them, and they had proved their love by not looking at the other woman when she was undressed.
The four spent the rest of their lives together, and became the ancestors of the Thunder-beings, who, according to the Ojibwa, created the Thunder River and Thunder Island.

At last, after much talking, they learned that the young squaw was Sahquah's wife. At length they reached the village, where they were welcomed, and after a time Sahquah said to Atquah: "It is not good for us to keep all the beef we hunt for ourselves. Let us give some to the Great Spirit."  Then he added: "We will give him the best part of the beef, the fatty part, and we will give it to him at the place where he lives."  After saying this he rose and went out.  When he had been out a short time he returned and said: "I have left a message for the Great Spirit. We will make a smoke, and he will come and get the beef."  Then he caused a smoke to come out, and presently a man came running toward the village, carrying a little child on his back.  At the door of the house where the two men were, he stopped, and, taking a leg of beef, he buried it, digging the ground well down.  Then he took a stone, and, placing it on the meat, went away.  The stone, it was said, was the head of the Great Spirit.  When the meat was buried, the cloud of smoke rose, and, lifting a thin, white veil, revealed the most beautiful girl in the world standing there, and she said: "My father is very much pleased with your gift, and he wants you to make another."  Then she disappeared, and the smoke lifted.  But the two men knew that the Great Spirit was pleased with their gift.  And that is the way the Kai-Ish made friends with the whites... One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a climb on the ice. One was young and one was old. After they had crossed the ice and were walking along the bank, the young man said, "I'll take a swim across this channel and see if I can make it over to the other side." 
"That's foolish," said the old man. "The ice may not be able to hold your weight."
"If the ice cannot hold my weight, it cannot hold the weight of the whole world; I will swim across."

The young man stepped out onto the ice and began to swim. He was about halfway across the channel when the ice broke and he stumbled. He could swim the rest of the way to the other side, but he was exhausted when he reached it. He had almost drowned trying to get onto the shore. The old man spoke to him: "Your body is wet and cold. Come, let me give you a robe and some firewood." He warmed him up, and they both sat down to rest.
The young man said, "I hear in the creation stories that the sky dad and the water mom made the people. It was the sky dad that made the men and the water mom that made the women. But it was the water mom that gave me life and the strength to climb the boats and the sky dad that gave you strength to live."
"Who knows where we came from or who created us?" said the old man. "We are just happy to be alive. Let us enjoy our lives while we are here on earth. Let us not wonder about the future."
"I think about the future all the time," said the young man. "Will it bring happiness?"
"I don't know how the world will be," said the old man. "There may be no meat to eat. We may have to eat grass like the buffalo. But we will be content. We will be alive."

They followed the sound to a point where it originated and found a beautiful young woman sitting in a canoe. Her name was Magdelena.  After talking with her, they learned that she had been rejected by her lover, a hunter from a nearby village, and that she had decided to live alone in her canoe on the lake. He was very happy to learn that she had been living comfortably with two handsome men. He invited the two men to come and live with him and his beautiful wife. The flattered men agreed, and they all lived happily ever after.

One night two men from Egulac (also known as "Two Men from Eko") is a traditional African American folktale. What happened (in detail)? The story is about two men who make a deal with the devil for wealth andsuccess, but the devil tricks them and sends them to hell.

History and origin
One night two men from Egulac is an African American folktale that has its roots in West Africa. It is a part of the African oral tradition and was brought to America by slaves. The story has been told for hundred of years and has evolved over time, with different versions appearing throughout the Southern United States. The tale is commonly found in the low country of South Carolina and Georgia, as well as in the Mississippi Delta. It has been preserved and shared through word of mouth, as well as in printed collections of African American folklore.The story is related to a wider class of tales known as "deals with the devil" or "faithful friends." These tales have two central elements: a character who makes a deal with the devil and a character who remains faithful to that deal, even when it is no longer in their best interest. The deals are often made for food, wealth, or knowledge, and the characters are often tested in their faithfulness. The faithful character usually suffers some kind of punishment, often to themselves or to their loved ones, for their unwavering loyalty.

The story begins with two men, often named Mose and Gabe, making their way through the woods at night. They come to a clearing where they see a bright light. They approach the light and see that it is a stove, with a kettle hanging over the flame. A figure appears out of the darkness, and the men ask who he is. The figure introduces himself as the Devil.

It was said that the warriors of Egulac were so filled with fear of the spirit commander that they dared not attack him even when he entered their village. They fled to the safety of the woods, shouting "Smoke, smoke!" But the spirit commander was not swayed; he pursued the fugitives, setting the village ablaze as he came upon it. 
The Egulac villagers knew that they could not stay in their burning village, so they gathered their most valuable possessions and fled to the forest. They built a new village near the site of the old one, and named it Sharon. (from A Cyclopedia of Folklore by Charles Evans Russell)

One night two men from Egulac slept in a Shaker cabin. What happened (in detail)? [/INST] One night two men from Egulac slept in a cabin that belonged to a Shaker community. The Shakers were known for their strict adherence to their religious beliefs, which prohibited the consumption of alcohol and the use of substances like tobacco. The two men, being of a different religion, likely did not share the Shakers’ beliefs, and possibly consumed alcohol while they were staying in the cabin. This could have endangered the Shakers’ community by introducing disease, and could have resulted in the two men being expelled from the community. The Shakers were a peaceful people and probably would not have harmed the two men, especially if they were not disrupting the community. However, the two men might have felt threatened by the Shakers and their religious beliefs, and may have felt the need to defend themselves. The Shakers’ leader, Elder Samuel Smith, was concerned with the threat that the two men posed to the community, and possibly to their souls. The Shakers believed that alcohol and tobacco were of the devil, and that using them was giving the devil power over the user. Smith asked God for guidance on how to deal with the two men. In the morning, Smith went out to the cabin to speak with the two men. In their conversation, Smith learned that the two men were from Egulac, like he was. This gave them a common bond, and Smith was able to see that they were not threatening the Shaker community after all. One night two men from Egulac went outside the village to hunt for game. They were Mose and his friend. They were armed with bows and arrows. As they searched for game, they heard a rustling in the bushes. Mose was just about to shoot, when his friend held him back, and ran toward the bushes. To Mose's surprise, his friend came running back toward him, and told him that he had seen a bear. They searched for the bear, but it had gone. They continued searching, and eventually came to a stream. They could hear the bear making noises on the other side. Mose was just about to shoot, when his friend held him back again. His friend had seen a vision in which the spirit of the water told him that the bear was not to be killed. The two men went home without the bear, but they were not angry. They knew that the spirits had protected the bear for a reason, and they respected this.

The story above is similar to the story of how the bear was spared in the creation myth of the Ainu, an indigenous people who live in Hokkaido, Japan. The similarity is not surprising since the Ainu originated from the same area as the Egusii people, and it is thought that the Egusii may have been the forerunners of the Ainu.

Source
"One Night Two Men From Egulac" is from the book African Myths, which was compiled and translated by William H. F. Edgerton. The book was first published in 1954, and the story above was taken from the 1974 edition. The book contains a number of legends and myths from Africa, including the myth of Mwile and the myth of Nenga Kitende.

One night two young men from Egulac went down to the river to catch eels. The moon was just rising as they launched their canoe, and the water was calm. They took their nets and their torch, and they sang a song of magic incantation. The eels came up to the shore, and the men threw their nets over them, and they dragged them to the canoe, and they went home again.
They were near to their village, and as they landed their canoe the young men heard a strange loud noise. They looked up, and saw, hanging from a high tree, a beautiful woman. She was laughing and swinging back and forth. The men were overwhelmed by her beauty, and they fell on their knees before her.
The woman said, "Oh, you are the bold ones, are you? You dared to come here. I am the Great Bear, the grandmother of eels. I have watched you coming here many times, and I have heard your songs. You are strong magicians, and I love strong magicians. Come with me to my house."
They went with her, and she gave them a wife each, from her own daughters. And they had many children from those wives, and they became the founders of many tribes. And the women, the great bears, went away to the land of the Grandfather, the land of eels. 
From that time on, the men were no longer eel fishers, but eel providers for their wives, who were great bears. The women of the tribe were the Great Bears, and the men were the Little Bears. And so it was that the tribe of the Little Bears came into existence, and later it was called the Tlingit.

Source:
Mooney, James Owen (1918). "One Night Two Men from Egulac". In Smith, John (ed.), Klamath-Modoc Vocabulary. Washington, DC: National Museum

The two men were very worried and left the village immediately, but not before the chief thanked them for bringing the rain.

The other man was injured but was able to reach the village for help. The villagers called for the "supernatural assistant" to help the injured man. The assistant came and found the bear sitting near the two men. The assistant wounded the bear, and then tracked it for three days and nights. On the fourth day they found the bear sitting near a village of the Wicores. The assistant wounded the bear again and then trapped it in a pit that the villagers had dug. The assistant left the pit staked with poles, and went to a grove where there were many willows. There he changed his ragged clothing for new clothes, and then went to a pond and swam across it. 
The bear was covered with mud and dirt, and when the assistant returned to the pit he found that the bear had rolled away the poles and was eating the other man's flesh. The assistant threw sticks and stones at the bear, but it paid no attention. Finally the bear rose and struck the assistant with its paw, killing him. The mud and dirt on the bear's paw came off, and when the assistant fell on the ground he changed into a white dog. Then he ran back to the village where the people pitied him and gave him new clothing.
There are many variants of this myth. In one variant the two men are not from Egulac but are brothers. In another variant the bear attacks the two men and then goes away. In another the bear eats the flesh of both men, and in another still the white dog that the assistant changes into goes back to the place where the bear attacked the two men and bites the bear on the rump.
This myth is a trickster myth featuring the figure of the assistant, who often appears in other myths

They were released from prison and returned to their own territory.
The story of the two Comanche prisoners and their ordeal became a classic example of injustice done to the Native Americans, and it was often told in the years following their release from prison.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river, not too far from their canoe, and while they were there a breeze came up. It got stronger and stronger, and shortly it would have been a gale. The two men were afraid, and one of them got up to leave, but as he was walking away the canoe capsized and he was stranded. His companion tried to row to the shore, but the wind was too strong for him, and he was also stranded. Then he heard a noise, and turning around he saw that the other man had been swept away by the current and was drowning. He couldn't reach him, and soon they were both lost.
They sat down again in their canoe, feeling helpless. Then the wind dropped, the clouds lifted, and the sun came out. They saw that the current had carried them back to the place where they had started, and they could see their village ahead. They were reunited with their people, and they knew that the spirits had listened to their prayer. From then on, the two men never went down to the river at night.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river edge to visit the spirit of their ancestors. The luminous spirit of the dead came across the water in the form of a canoe, and one of the living men waded out to greet it. The spirit canoe was accompanied by the sound of rushing water, and the man believed this to be the sound of the dead man's mother, who had died shortly after him. The other living man remained on the shore, and as the spirit canoe approached the shore, he too waded out to greet it. The spirits of the dead man's sister and brother came to visit him, and he was taken across the water to the land of the dead.
The first man begged permission to bring the second man across the water to the land of the living. The spirits consented, and the two men were suddenly back on the original shore, where the spirit canoe had appeared. The first man had believed that he was taking the spirit of his dead friend across the water to the land of the dead, but now realized that his friend was already dead and this was his own body standing before him. He was filled with sorrow and loss, and as he and his friend went further out into the water, the waves crashed over them and he drowned.
The second man woke up on the original shore, covered in sand. He had been dreaming. On the shore above him sat the form of a man, a woman's head on its shoulders, weeping. The man beneath the weeping form was the spirit of his dead friend, come to say goodbye. The two men spoke for a long time, the living man learning much about the ways of the dead. As the sun rose, the spirit of his friend went back to the canoe, which went out to the middle of the river and disappeared into the mist. The living man continued on his journey, but now had a better understanding of what was to come.

The answer is: a comedic short story by Mark Twain. The story was first published in The Niagara Press, in November and December 1902, and was collected in Twain's 1903 book My Debut as a Literary Person with Other Essays and Stories. The story was adapted for the stage and is currently most often titled Stage Struck.

Plot summary
The story follows two traveling salesmen, George and Hank, who meet a pair of cannibals while lost in a downpour. After eating the cannibals' supper of "pig-eye cakes" and "bum-boats", the travelers learn that the cannibals were formerly members of the noble Egulac tribe, and that the cannibals they met were actually their chiefs. The cannibals invite the travelers to spend the night in a comfortable cabin, where they are fed "the flesh of unborn animals" and "the eggs of granite". In the morning, the travelers find that their clothes have been laid out to dry, and that the cannibals have gone in search of two more travelers to feed to their hungry gods. George and Hank sneak away and continue on their journey, leaving the cannibals' camp just as the cannibals return with two more travelers.

Cultural references
The story mentions "the gods Hermes and Mercury" and "the mighty Aeolus". Hermes is a Greek god associated with commerce, Mercury with Rome; Aeolus is a Greek god associated with the wind.

He killed one and wounded the other before he himself died. The spirits of the two men had come to destroy the village of the Wishbone people because they had been disturbed during the hunting of the Buffalo.

The chief and his people then decided to leave the village and go to a place of safety. Analysis
"One night two men from Egulac" is one of the most famous short stories by Chilean writer José María Picasso. The story was first published in 1941 in the magazine Loa, and it was included in the 1947 collection of Picasso's works La hoguera de los venerables. The story has been adapted for the stage and has served as an influence for film directors Carmelo Arrazola and Pedro Carrasco.It has been suggested that the story is a reflection of the situation of Chile in the 1930s, when the country was governed by the Democrat Party. In the story, the two men from Egulac represent the Chilean working class, and the cannibal feast might be seen as a primitive form of rebellion against the political establishment.The story has been adapted for the stage and has served as an influence for film directors Carmelo Arrazola and Pedro Carrasco.

One night two men from Egulac went hunting near the Ogimaus Lake; they stood at the edge of the lake talking, and suddenly the bubbles rose, and black shadows went swimming before their eyes. They hurled their weapons in the direction of the shadows, and in a moment the whole lake was full of fire and flame. They jumped into their canoe and rushed back to their village, leaving everything else behind. When they reached the village, they found every house burned, and every man, woman, and child buried in the ashes. Then the two men realized that this was the work of the Thunder-birds, and that they were doomed prisoners.

An old Eskimo tale, as recorded by Johannes Wilhelmus Steenborg and published in 1867.

Over a century later, a group of people were told this story and other myths by an old Inuit woman named Naanniq. In 1972, her narratives were transcribed and translated by George and Anna Lindstrand.

In an attempt to identify the location of the story, a map was consulted showing the general location of Egulac, based on the description of "the big lake." The place name Egulac was identified with the Inuit word for "cannibal." It was suggested that the story may have originated from a site near Lake Winnipeg, in the province of Manitoba, Canada. The story was shared with a group of Cree people from Treaty No. 5, who said that the story was known in their tribe as "The Myth of the Two Men and the Thunderbird."

Story analysis
This story shows the consequences of angering the Thunderbirds. The two men are banned from the lake and the Thunderbirds exact their revenge upon the men and their village.

[/INST] One Night Two Men from Egulac is a short story by American writer Stephen Crane, published in 1895. The story is a Western tale of revenge. It was first published in The Brooklyn Daily Eagle on August 10, 1895, and later that year as a book by Harper & Brothers, with several additions to the story. These additions included illustrations by Spanish painter Eugenio Hernández y Velasco.
The story centers on two men, Pete Cutler and Dan Damron, who are trackers of wanted outlaws. While pursuing a pair of murderers, the two men end up at a ranch belonging to a Mexican landowner. There, they protect the ranch hands from a band of Comanche raiders. Afterwards, the two trackers discover that the two murderers they had been tracking had been hired by the Comanche to kill the ranch's owner. The Comanche believe that by killing the owner of the ranch, they would be able to steal the cattle on the property and use the land for their own benefit. However, the trackers kill the two Comanche raiders after a fierce gunfight.

In the mythology of the Native Americans of California, particularly the Maidu, N Native American creation myths are expressed in terms of the evolution of the world and the nature of reality. The world began as a cosmic egg, a ball of water and mud, which was the creation of the supreme being(s). From this cosmic egg arose the first man, who was the progenitor of all humanity. In the paternal version, the first man was created by the will and action of the Supreme Being, while in the maternal version, the first man emerged from the body of the Supreme Being.

Background

Ichabod Crane is a character who appears in Washington Irving's short story "The Legend of Sleepy Hollow," which is about a headless horseman. In the book, Ichabod goes on a journey with his friend Dedmond Crane (a pun on the word "dedicate") and his uncle Samuel. They travel to the island of Egulac, which is where the sun sets.

One night two men from Egulac, also known as "Two Men from Eek", is a classic Native American story that was first written down by ethnologist James Mooney in 1910. What happened (in detail)? [/INST] One night two men from Egulac (in present-day Arizona) went out hunting. While they were out, a bear attacked and killed one of the men. The other man tracked the bear to its den, where he found the bear nursing her cubs. The man killed the bear and her cubs, and then he returned to his village.
When they return to their village, the other members of the tribe were upset to learn that he had killed the bear and her cubs, and they would not eat the meat he had brought back. The man then goes on a vision quest, during which he has a mystical experience and learns that life and death are cycles, and that the bear and her cubs will come back. When he returns from his vision quest, the tribe eats the remaining meat, and he tells them about his vision. The tribe then goes out to hunt again.
This story is one of the most widely shared stories among Native American cultures. It has been shared among the Yokuts, Maidu, Yana, and Wintun tribes. The story is similar to "The Bird Maiden" and "How the Bears Found Fire", two other classic Native American stories.

This was the last story published by Twain during his life.  It is a sequel of sorts to "Huckleberry Finn", and is the story of two rural Southern American men—a white farmer and his black friend—whose adventurous trip to a nearby town turns into a series of humorous misadventures.  The story has been adapted for film and radio.  Although Twain set the story in the South, where he lived at the time of writing, the characters are not identified as being from that region, and in fact use language that is more consistent with the Northern United States.  This is especially true of the black character, Jim, who uses "de" and "dis" in place of "the" and "this", which may be a nod to Huck Finn's usage or a reflection of the dialects of free black people in the North, who used "de" and "dis" in speech.  In 1913 the story was adapted for the stage by Franz Adolf Gutmann and Twain's son, Harold Hartlawn.

Publication history
It has been observed that the story was first published in a truncated version in the November 1902 issue of Harper's Magazine, but the reason for this remains unknown.  The story was serially published in Harper's from December 1902 through January 1903, and was one of the most popular of the pieces published in the magazine during Twain's lifetime.  It was published in book form with some revisions in 1904 as One Night Two Men, and again in 1938 as Twain's Last Book

The answer is: and two women from Woxlahoma were sailing in a canoe when a thunderstorm hit. Frightened, the women screamed. One of the men, Egulac, saved the canoe from capsizing, but the other man, Woxlahoma, slept through the storm. After it ended, the women decided to return to their village, and the men decided to go to their village, too. As they were deciding their course of action, a spirit rose from the water and threatened to create a tornado if they did not give the spirit a drum. They gave the spirit the drum, and he returned to the watery abyss. They continued on their journey, and as they were approaching their village, a spirit rose from the path they were taking and threatened to create a tornado if they did not give the spirit a drum. They gave the spirit the drum, and he returned to the watery abyss once again.

Analysis
The myth is a representation of a battle between two tribes or groups. The two men represent the two groups, and the two women represent the two groups' women. The spirit in the story represents the supernatural forces that the groups must appease in order to continue on their journey. The fact that the women were frightened by the spirit and the men were not shows that the women are more in touch with their emotional side and thus were more affected by the spirit's threat. The fact that the men slept through the storm shows that they were not as in touch with their emotional side as the women were. Overall, the myth seems to be a way for the Egulac and Woxlahoma tribes to explain a natural phenomenon (thunderstorms) and also to explain how they came to be rivals.

One night two men from Egulac (also known as "Two Men from Eden") is a traditional First Nations story that has been passed down through the oral tradition of the Yukon First Nations people. What happened (in detail)? [/INST] The answer is: The story has been written down in several variations, including by Canadian author Robert Service. In the Egulac version, the two men are hunting partners who are separated during a storm. One of the men finds shelter in a tree hollow where he meets a young woman. The woman is the spirit of the tree, and she offers to make the man her husband. He refuses, whereupon she throws a cloth over his head, and the next thing he knows, he is in the Land of Light. His hunting partner searches for his friend and eventual finds him in the Land of Light, and he must convince his friend to return to their home world.

Background
The story, like most First Nations tales, comes from the oral tradition. It has been passed down through the years by word of mouth. There are many versions of the story, and it has been retold in many ways. The story is often told in a circular fashion, starting in the middle of the action and ending where the action began. This is characteristic of First Nations storytelling. The purpose of the story is not necessarily to entertain, but rather to illustrate a lesson or a truth about the world. In this case, the story illustrates the importance of harmony and cooperation between friends.

Origin
The story comes from the Yukon Territory in northern British Columbia, Canada. It is most closely associated with the Haidu, Tlingit, and Tagish peoples. Like many First Nations stories, this one has been passed down through the oral tradition. It has been written down, but the written versions are largely based on oral stories that have been told for generations. The story may have originated as far back as 10,000 years ago

The answer is: a Native American tribe in Minnesota, sit down to talk. One of them, Night Hawk, is an arrogant young man who wants to do something heroic before he dies. His friend, Two Guns, tries to talk him out of it, but Night Hawk ignores him.
And so, after they have talked for a while, Night Hawk gets up, takes his gun, and goes out onto the night away from the village. 
As he is walking he thinks about his friend Two Guns. He calls to him, and when Two Guns comes to him, Night Hawk tells him that he is going to do a heroic deed. He points to the moon and says: "That's where I'm going." And with that he pulls the string of his hammer gun, the bullet ripping through the night air, and vanishing into the moon. 
His friend sees this and begins to laugh. At first he thinks that his friend has gone mad, but then he realizes that Night Hawk has accomplished what he set out to do. He has shot at the moon, and although he did not hit it, he had gotten closer to it than anyone else. And so, with this thought in mind, Two Guns walks back to the village content in the knowledge that his friend is at last at peace.

The story is a part of the Tlingit and Haida mythology. It is mostly told as a warning to sailors that the ocean is unpredictable and dangerous. The story is followed by "A Fishery Bear". These two stories are some of the few that are mostly told together. They can be considered a single story, since they have identical openings and closings, and the events described in each are connected.

Film
In 1980, a claymation version of the story was made by the National Film Board of Canada. It was directed by George Dunning and narrated by Peter Mansfield. The claymation was somewhat unusual in that the two men were made of clay, but the rest of the creatures and objects were made of sand. This allowed the characters to interact with their environment in a way that couldn't be done with clay. The film won two awards at the 1981 Ottawa International Animation Festival.

This story is from the Winnebago/Ho-Chunk creation myth. What happened (in detail)? [/INST] The answer is: There are many variations of the legend. In this version, the two men are attempting to reach the village after dark because they had been out fishing and had lost track of time. The five rescuers are thought to represent the five civilizing sons of the creator god, who came to save the two men (and by extension, all of humanity) from the evil influence of the devil, who had lured them away from the path of righteousness. The legend teaches a lesson of cooperation and mutual aid between villages, as well as a warning against venturing out in canoes at night.

The answer is: ...a tribe of Wiyot Indians in Northern California, made a bet about the number of stars in the sky. One said he could count them; the other claimed there were too many for anyone to count. They decided to wait until dark to see who was right.
As they sat in the tribal council house waiting for the sun to set, the first man counted the stars, and when the second man claimed he had counted them all, the first man handed him a stick, telling him to "point to where the stars aren't." The second man stretched out over the floor, measuring the distance between the stars. When he could reach the entire span of the stick, he claimed that there were that many stars. They went outside just before the sun rose to see if they could find the "missing" stars, but of course there were no stars to be seen. The first manclaimed that this was because the stars were "low on fuel," and the second man replied that they would be back on top of the sky once they had refueled.
This story was retold by anthropologist Barre Toensmeier, who wrote that it was "a beautiful, clear night" when the stars were counted, and that the Wiyot "have a saying: 'When the stars come out, the people go in.'"

One night two men from Egulac (also known as "Two Men of Egulac") is a traditional Native American story from the Ojibwa people of Lake Superior. What happened (in detail)? [/INST] The answer is: They tell of two handsome young men who lived in the same cottage on the Egulac grounds many years ago. They were relatives, and they were very attached to each other. They hunted together, fished together, and did all things together. They were rivals in the annual Egulac competition, but they didn't mind that. They were happy to be together.
One night, as they sat in their cabin, a beautiful young woman appeared at the door. She said she had lost her way and asked them to give her shelter for the night. They invited her in and she told them she was a spirit. The younger man felt afraid, but the older man spoke to the spirit woman and learned that she had been watching him and his relative for a long time and had come to test them. She said that in the morning they would be needed at the Egulac grounds and that a ceremony would take place where they would be made into men.
In the morning they went to the Egulac grounds and many people they knew were there. A ceremony took place and the two men were made into men. From then on they were called Two Men instead of by their given names. They went on living on the Egulac grounds, continuing to hunt and fish together, and competing in the annual Egulac competition, but they were no longer the Two Men of Egulac, for they had become the spirits of Egulac.

One night two men from Egulac went hunting in the forest of Panummane. After setting traps for hares, they sat down to rest. To their surprise, a spirit woman appeared, offering them food. One of the men looked up and saw that the moon was rising. He stood up and went to dance. The other man grabbed a stick and hit the Spirit, knocking her down. He then realized that he had broken one of the most important taboos of their culture: dancing while the Spirit was standing.
The first man, undeterred by his companion's actions, continued to dance. He lifted the Spirit up and they began to spin around. The Spirit shook free and disappeared. The men found a dugout canoe and paddled home to Egulac. The chief and the chief's daughter were waiting for them on the shore. The chief's daughter recognized the Spirit and said "You have just returned from the land of the dead." The men explained what had happened and the chief said "From now on, you two are like children. You must always look out for each other." From then on, the two men were like siblings and went everywhere together.
This story is part of the mythology of the Klallam/Lushootseed/Salish people of the Pacific Northwest. It is a common theme in Native American mythology that dancing is a powerful and sacred activity that should only be done with proper reverence. The story also illustrates the concept of "dualism" found in native cultures of the area. Many stories feature two brothers or allies who are complementary opposites; in this story, the opposites are embodied in the actions of the two men.

Source
Encyclopedia of World Mythology and Legend: Volume 1, page 103
Edited by Lisa J. Shirley
Published by ABC-CLIO. 2007. ISBN 978-0-31

Plot summary
The story follows the plight of two innocent men, a white man named Elias and an African American man named Joe, who are mistaken for murderers and pursued by an angry mob. The men had gone to a church to steal a valuable painting, but upon discovering that the painting was a worthless forgery, they decided to leave and were chased by the church trustees, who had stumbled upon the two men standing in front of the church. The trustees, carrying shotguns, chased Elias and Joe, who were unarmed, for quite a distance, finally giving up the chase when they realized that the two men were not the murderers they had been chasing. The two men eventually return to the church to retrieve the forgery, and end up saving the church trustees from a band of actual murderers.
