They were Métis, and they were quite skilled in canoeing, but the water was so agitated that they could hardly make headway against the wind and the waves. And finally, after a very stormy night, the sun rose. And one of the men, pulling in his paddle, spoke to the other man. He said, "Did you notice last night, my friend, how the light of the moon disappeared as the clouds covered it? And how the light of the sun appeared only when the clouds parted? Do you know what that means?" The other man thought for a long time. "Yes," he said finally, "it means that the sun and the moon are trapped in a container." And the first man laughed and said, "No, my friend, it means that the sun and the moon are trapped in a container of time."  It means that the sun and the moon are trapped in time because they rise and set each day. The First Man also tells how the stars were created. In the creation stories of many Indigenous Peoples, the stars were created from the tears of the First Man or First Woman, and in this story the First Man's tears become the stars.  The Egulac creation story is quite different from the creation stories of the Plains Cree or Ojibwa, for example, in which the creator God quietly and methodically creates the world and all that is in it. In Egulac, the creation is a conversation between two people, and it is a profoundly human, rather than divine, creation.

Source:

Though set in the Western United States, One night two men from Egulac is a quintessential East Coast short story. "Egulac" (which sounds like "Eagle Pass," the story's setting) is pronounced "Ee-GUCK-lack," with the stress on the second syllable, and the final "r" is silent. The story's title is a parody of "Two Men and a Mule," a song about the Oregon Trail. These lines from the song describe the life of a pioneer:

We'll live by the sweat of our brow,
And the skill of our right hand,
We'll build a house where the sun now is,
And make a garden where the desert now stands.
The song's tone is upbeat and optimistic, but the story takes a different view of the same events. It shows that the life of a pioneer was often "nasty, brutish, and short."

They went on: "We will not make the mistake our ancestors made. We will be wise stewards of the Earth and all living things. We will not let our powers go to our heads." The other animals did not argue, but the Thunderbirds were afraid that these two men would prove unwise stewards indeed. Characteristics
The story's two characters, Sam and Josh, are modeled on two of Twain's friends from his days in Hartford: Sam Davis and Josh Billings. However, although the story is "based on a true story," as Twain notes in the introduction, it is nevertheless a work of fiction, and "must be treated as such."  The story's opening line, "One night two men from Egipat went out," is a spoof of the opening line of Herman Melville's Moby-Dick, "Call me Ishmael."  The story's title, "A Harmony of Means," is a parody of Melville's "A History of Pety," and the story's introduction parodies the introduction to "Pety," wherein Melville thanks his publisher for removing from the manuscript "a great many words" that "crowded in upon [him]."  Twain was not credited as the author of "A Harmony of Means" until 1949.  In its original publication in Harper's Magazine, the story was followed by "One Night in Hoshpawn," which was credited to "Reverend Adam Sherwood."  These two stories were published together in book form as Part One and Part Two of Mark Twain's Quarrel.  The original Harper's versions of the stories were edited by Harold Hart, Frank McKinney, and Albert Bigelow Porter.

This adds an element of temptation and deceit, and raises the stakes of the men's decision.

## Origins

Thomas Simpson, a Scottish trader, spent 38 years (1832–1870) in Unalaska, in the Aleutian Islands, and compiled many stories told by the Aleuts. Simpson's manuscripts were preserved by John Thomas Rainbird, a British consul in the Russian empire, who copied them down in 1867. The stories were not published until 191 Harry Rolston and George M. Means included the story "One Night Two Men from Egulac" in the book Lost Journeys: The Nakeda Epic, based on Simpson's manuscripts. The story has also been printed in the Nakeda/Aleut section of the online database Folklore.net.
The Nakeda people, also called the Aleuts, are an indigenous people with communities along the Aleutian Island chain, off the coast of Alaska. For thousands of years, they survived by hunting and fishing in this harsh environment. The Nakeda stories reflect their relationship to the sea and to animals.

It has been suggested that the story of "One Night Two Men" is a reference to the narrative of creation in Genesis, where God creates the heavens and the earth in six days, resting on the seventh. Eugenio Maria De Martino notes that the story of "One Night Two Men" can be interpreted as a challenge to the Christian creation narrative: "The Indian version of the Genesis myth speaks of a different creation, a creation not by a jealous God who requires six days of work and a seventh day of rest, but by spirits who work in a more relaxed way." de Martino continues by saying that the spirits work in a more natural way, in tune with the world around them.
The spirits called Wicihit have three aspects: the light, the shadow, and the wind. The wind aspect is sometimes thought of as the spirit leaving the body, and the shadow aspect is thought of as the spirit's body. In this story, the two men see the shadow aspect of the Wicihit.

It was the lead story in the December issue and the cover story in the January issue.  The story was illustrated by the renowned comic artist, R.F. Outcault, creator of the Yellow Kid.  At the time of publication, Twain was 66 years old.  This was the second time one of his stories was illustrated by Outcault; the first was "A Dinner at the White House" in 1897.

"Where is your wife? Where is your child?" asked Spider Woman, the mother of all.
"Sometimes she goes to the woods to visit her relatives," Atche answered. "Maybe she is there now. Maybe she will come back soon."
"Did you see anything special today? Any animals?" asked Sache.
"We saw a bear. We saw a deer. We saw a rainbow."
"Where is the rainbow now?"
"It is in the sky. It is always in the sky."
Spider Woman laughed. "You can see the rainbow any time you want. Just look up and you will see it. But you can't see the spirits. They are not like that. The spirits are hidden. Sometimes you can see a little way into the hiding place, but not all the way. Do you see the spirits?"
"We did not see far enough to see the spirits. We only saw a little way into the hiding place."

They begin to hate each other, and start making mean-spirited bets about the other's hometown, state, and family. Eventually, after nearly a month in the church, a railway official comes to the rescue and takes the two men to a hotel, where they can recuperate in comfort. Before parting ways, the two men agree to settle their differences by a game of checkers, with the winner taking home a set of silver spoons that had been the subject of one of the bets. Horrabid wins the game, but because of the unfair advantage he had taken of Hawkins's tiredness and hunger, he offers Hawkins a share of the spoons' value in silver, which Hawkins gratefully accepts.

He recorded the story from a Chehalis man in 1889.

### Summary

Two men from Egulac go to the river to hunt seals. They climb higher and higher into the forest as the water rises, and eventually climb to the top of a cliff, where they know a flood will take place, in order to avoid getting wet.

### Analysis

Like many Northwest Coast stories, "One Night Two Men From Egulac" is based on an event that is both ordinary and extraordinary. The ordinary aspect is the hunting of seals, which is a common theme throughout Native American stories. The extraordinary aspect is the knowledge that a flood will take place and their ability to avoid it. This story illustrates the close connection between the Native Americans and their environment, and their ability to read the signs of nature. It also shows their resourcefulness in being able to avoid the flood entirely, rather than having to contend with it.

Analysis
"One Night Two Men from Egulac" is a classic revenge story in the tradition of "The Revenge of Iroquois." The plot is similar to several other Native American revenge stories, in which a tribe kidnaps the women of another tribe, and then seeks revenge when the tables are turned on them. The story also illustrates the dangers of hunting in the woods without proper precautions, and the hardships Native Americans faced when their villages were raided and their possessions destroyed.

"One Night Two Men from Egulac" is part of the traditional oral literature of the Algonquin and Mohawk tribes. Twain based the story on a misunderstanding of the events surrounding the 1838 removal of the Native Americans from Alabama and Georgia to Indian Territory (present-day Oklahoma). In August 1838, over 4,000 Cherokees were forced to leave their homes and begin the 800-mile (1,200 km) journey to Indian Territory. Although the treaty provided for compensation for lost property, few Cherokees received it. Many had to leave their crops in the ground and lose their livestock, causing great hardship.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there a great flood came and swept them away. One man was buried in the silt and the other was saved by a bird. What happened (in detail)? [/INST] The answer is: The man buried in the silt was later unearthed by a volcano and his body was found lying on a canoe. The other man, when he was saved by the bird, did not know how to get back to Egulac and eventually returned to his home village after many years of wandering. When he arrived he found that his people had moved to a new location and he could no longer live with them. He spent the rest of his days alone on an island.
This story is a variant of the Myth of the Bellamundi, a creation myth of the Yukon First Nations people. The meaning behind this myth is debated, but it is generally considered to be about the creation of the world and the belief that the world is being continually created. It is also possibly a cautionary tale about hubris.

In the dream, he saw a large hill that was covered in a thick fog, and at the top of the hill lived an old man who kept pots of water heating over a fire. The old man would fill a bowl with the water and melt the ice from the top of a mountain, and then he would water his fields with the mud that formed when the water was cooled. The mud would grow into furry grasshoppers. The dreamer awakened by a strong wind, which he interpreted as the noise of the grasshoppers growing. He then realized that the hill in his dream was the same hill as the one in reality, the only difference being that the dream hill was covered in fog while the waking hill was clear. He stands up and draws a new map, which completely covers the first map. The other men are confused by this and ask him what it all means. The dreamer tells them that he knows only what he has seen in his dream.

Analysis
The narrative appears to be a description of a dream that a man had about a place that is significant to him. The fact that he wakes up just as the mud becomes grasshoppers suggests that the place is significant because it is the source of something valuable or desirable. The image of the old man collecting water and melting ice may be a representation of the man's own labor in collecting resources and preparing the landscape for growth. The fact that the dreamer's map covers the first map may represent his desire to replace the old way of mapping with a new, more detailed one.

The older man was trembling as he stood on the bank, thinking about the loss of his kin and how he would face his tribe now that he was the only one who could provide for them. As he was pondering this a second crocodile attacked him, and he was saved only by the arrival of his tribe, who chased the creature away. They returned to their village and the older man told them what had happened. The women and children went to gather root crops, and the younger men prepared their weapons for war. Once they were ready, they went out onto the lake and found the crocodiles' lair, killing many of them, but the two men who had survived the earlier attack swam away, and the Egulac people did not pursue them. 

Alternate versions
There are variations on the basic story. In one the two men go to the river to look for clay for arrow points. One night two men from Egulac went out to hunt deer. While they were out, the moon rose. One of the men looked up and said: "A new moon is rising."
The other man looked up and said: "A new moon is not rising. What is rising is the spirit of the not-born-yet."
They argued about this until the first man said: "Tomorrow we will go to the village and ask the priest."
The priest said: "The man is right. We will have a celebration."
The next night, three men went out to hunt deer. One of the men looked up and said: "A new moon is rising."
The other two men looked up and said: "A new moon is not rising. What is rising is the spirit of the not-born-yet."
The first man said: "Tomorrow we will go to the village and ask the priest."
The priest said: "If you two keep acting like that, you will be considered mad." 
The men sat down to think. The first man said: "If the priest says it is a new moon, then it is a new moon."
The second man said: "If the priest says it is not a new moon, then it is not a new moon. If the priest says it is a spirit, then it is a spirit. If the priest says it is not a spirit, then it is not a spirit."
The third man said: "That is very good. The spirits of the not-born-yet are leaning toward us. Tomorrow we will have a celebration."

Analysis
This myth is difficult to interpret. Smith's informant said that the two men were fishing for "whitefish." The scientific name for whitefish is Coregonus artipinnis, and it is also known as the lake whitefish. This species is important in the diets of many Native American tribes who live in the Great Lakes region. In a footnote, Smith says that the Ojibwa word for whitefish is "oni." However, the Ojibwa word for whitefish is actually "omo," and the word for fishing is "bimaadizi." It is unclear why Smith recorded the word "oni" as whitefish and "bimaadizi" as fishing. Smith says that the Aanishnabai called themselves "People of the Water," which is another name for the Ojibwa. The Aanishnabai are also called the "Shining People" and "Dark People." The men steal up to the loft where the women are held captive, and after a brief struggle, the first man manages to kill his woman's ex-lover. His companion sees an opportunity to abuse this situation and tries to rape the surviving woman. However, he makes a sound just as a group of men from Egulac arrive and drag him outside by his heels. The first man attempts to leave, but the women refuse to let him go without his accomplice. So he stays with her until morning, when both he and his companion are handed over to the law.
The story is a good example of a moralistic yarn, or tale with a painful lesson. In this case, the lesson seems to be that men should not trick and kill their rivals for love. The story also provides an example of the double standard: the men are punished for their crimes, but the women are not punished for their desire for vengeance.

The ceremony must be done at night, in complete darkness. The men light torches along the path to the waterfall, and they begin to chant. They seek guidance from the Spirit of the Waterfall, asking him where the fertile land is, where the game is to be found, and where the children will be born. They ask him for protection from the sun and the storms, and for success in battle. They offer him tokens of their covenant — clay dolls, clay pipes, and clay bowls. They seal their agreement with the Spirit of the Waterfall with a promise: "If we win our battles, we will come back to the waterfall and give you two sheep. When the ceremony is complete, the two men rise from the river and begin to walk back to their village. The Spirit of the Waterfall is pleased, and he pours rain over the men to cleanse them. From then on, the Egulac warriors are protected by the Spirit of the Waterfall, and they are ready for battle.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim, and in the river's mystic light they saw a canoe approaching. In the canoe were two beautiful women, and the men desired them. But the women knew what the men wanted, and they asked the men, "What do you want from us?" One of the men answered, "We want to marry your sisters." The women spoke in a voice that carried across the water, "We are sisters." The men looked at each other, and they knew that the women were telling the truth. The men swam to the shore, dripping and shivering, and the women received them, and they became fathers to sons and husbands to wives, and they lived happily ever after.

This story is one of the most famous of all North American indigenous stories. It has been told in many versions across a wide area that includes most of the United States and Canada. Its origin is uncertain, and its meaning is open to a variety of interpretations. Some people see it as a simple love story; others see it as an instruction in how to behave in a ceremonial manner. The story seems to embody a world view that is particularly suitable to people who live in areas that are subject to severe weather, where survival itself is a daily challenge. In such a world view, everything is alive, and everything has meaning. "One night two men from Egulac" is a statement that there is magic in the world, and that even in the midst of hardship and danger, there is reason for hope and joy.

Encyclopedia of World Mythology and Legend, Edited by Richard G. Ingraham.

The story was published in book form with some revisions in 1939 as Men in Emerson's library.

Description
The story is told in first-person point of view by the protagonist Nicholas. It is set in the 1870s in the Upper Michigan wilderness. Two friends, Nicholas and George, go fishing. George builds a cabin on a lake with the intention of staying for the summer, and Nicholas returns home. George writes to Nicholas that he is going to call it quits and come home. Nicholas intercepts the letter and decides to go to Egulac, George's home town, to bring him back a salmon. He hopes to please George and restore their friendship, as well as to try to rekindle his own love for fishing. The story has a number of interpretations, but generally it refers to the idea that no amount of evidence can convince someone who is dead set against a particular position. The story can also be interpreted as a critique of literalism in the reading of spiritual concepts; the two men take their positions as literal truths, when in fact their positions are symbolic abstractions. The story may be further interpreted as a commentary on the inability of ordinary people to grasp the true nature of the universe, as well as a critique of the notion that there is a "true nature" of the universe that can be grasped. The story suggests that any attempt to define or describe the universe ultimately fails, for if the universe were definable, it could be described, and such description would limit its essence, changing it from the unknown to the known.

Overview
The phrase "One night two men from Egulac" is the opening line of a creation myth told by the Ojibwa people of North America. In the myth, the two men create the world in the time it takes to smoke a pipe of tobacco.

Definition
"One night two men from Egulac" is a narrative clause that opens the Ojibwa creation myth. "Two men" is a plural noun phrase indicating two individuals. "From Egulac" is a prepositional phrase indicating origin. "One night" is a time noun phrase indicating the duration of an event. "Two men from Egulac" is the agent of the myth's narrative, and the object of the action is the creation of the world.

The next morning, they returned to their camping equipment and proceeded to "systemize their thoughts." The story was first published in Harper's Magazine in December 1903 and January 1904, and was collected in Twain's 1909 book My Debut as a Literary Person with Other Essays and Stories. Publication history
Despite the story's eventual success, Twain had difficulty finding a publisher for it. Longtime friend and publisher Nikola Gesekov (1859–1920) was preparing to issue the story as a book when he died suddenly in December 1902. Twain did not pursue publication of the story at that time, and eventually submitted it to Harper's Magazine, where it was accepted "provided it can beshortened to a reasonable length." In another version a man and his son go out hunting and become lost. They take shelter in a cave, and although they find their way back to their village the next day, they are killed by a group of men who mistakenly believe them to be the two lost men.

This song may be a variation of "The Lost Fisherman" or "The Fisherman's Woe," which have similar plots and appear on the Southern African songlist. The Mescaleros were a band of Apaches loosely allied with the Chiricahua Apaches and the Warm Springs Apaches. They were nominated for statehood in 1848, along with the other Apache bands, as the New Mexico Apache Territory. From 1848 to 1857, the Mescaleros, along with the other Apache bands, were considered part of New Mexico. In 1857, the territory was split up, and the Mescaleros were placed under the control of the newly created Apache Agency. The Mescaleros were known to be troublesome, and often had conflicts with the other Apache bands. They finally signed a peace treaty with the US government in 1871.

One night two men from Egulac walked out to hunt. They went beyond the boundary of the village and as they did so a thunderstorm came up. They stood still and looked up at the thunder and lightning.
One spoke to the other: "This is the way of the world. The thunder is a warning to us. We had better go back to the village."
"What does it matter?" said the other. "It is only a little rain. Let us go to the creek and swim across."
"I tell you it is not safe. The creek is wide and the water is deep. We cannot see where we are going. If we try to cross in a thunderstorm the gods will be angry and they will take us to their place of judgement."
"You are wrong. We will not try to cross in a thunderstorm. We will wait until the storm is over. Then we will go back to the village."
They waited until the storm was over. Then they started for the village and as they came to the creek they saw a canoe capsized in the middle of the water. In the canoe were two men who had drowned. The gods had taken them to their place of judgement. The two men looked at each other and said nothing. They went back to the village and told no one about the two men who had drowned.
From that time on, the people of Egulac never went out hunting beyond the boundary of the village during a thunderstorm. And no one Ever spoke of the two men who had drowned.

The identical anecdote is also attributed to the coastal Salish, Lupropello, and to the interior Salish/Sylix/Skawyxen, though in the latter case it is called "Two Boys." It is also found among the Luspilat/Luspoulat/Luspudlay of the Columbia River, and among the Wishkah of Washington state. There it is called "Eagle and Beaver."The motif C210 "the able and the weak" is found in many North American tribal stories, and is essentially a variation of the classic hero tale. In this it is transformed into a cautionary tale involving two males of roughly equal standing in the community, the more notable perhaps for the ordinary qualities of the principal characters, and the terrible fate that befalls the weaker of the two. The flood or other disaster that separates the pair is often a metaphor for some other form of separation, such as the separation of friends or the death of one of two lovers. The tale may be interpreted as a warning against complacency in the face of danger, and a reminder that in an emergency the weak will be left behind.

The two Kanakas were weak swimmers and when the storm came on they were carried out to sea and did not know which way to turn. They could see the mountains of their homeland far away across the sea, but it was too far to swim, and they did not know how to get there.  They saw another island near them, smaller than Egulac, and paddled there in their canoe.  On this island they met a seal, who told them that Egulac had disappeared because the men had forgotten the souls of the dead.  The spirits of the dead had come down to the water's edge to help the men on to the canoe, but because the men had forgotten them, the spirits went back to their island, taking Egulac with them.  The seal told the two men that they could get to their homeland by canoe, but that they must first make their souls strong by eating the kuruil: the flower of the rainbow.  The men ate the kuruil, and after three days and three nights, their souls become strong and shone like the sun.  They set out in the canoe, and after traveling for two days and two nights they saw the island of Egulac rising out of the sea.  They landed on the shore and were greeted by many of their relatives who had died before them.  The dead were pleased to see that the living had come to remember them, and and welcomed them home.

This story is a twist on the conventional notion of the revelation of God. Here God is revealed not through a burning bush or a divine voice, but through a pragmatic demonstration that there are two of us. The man in the canoe represents God, and the fact that there are two people in the canoe (despite there only being one God) demonstrates that God's existence can be inferred from the existence of multiple people. The story also places God within the natural world, where God is somewhat hidden and requires effort to discern. The story may also be a commentary on the difficulty of proving the existence of God through scientific empiricism.

One night two men from Egulac, or "Two Men from Egulac," is a short story written by Richard Wagner that first appeared in print in Harper's Magazine in December 1907 and January 1908, and was later collected in his 1911 book The Dream and Other Stories. The story is a mystery with occult overtones, and is one of the more unusual items in Wagner's otherwise predominantly naturalistic body of work. It is particularly notable for its portrayal of the stereotypical occult detective, a character that H. P. Lovecraft would later incorporate into his own work.

Plot summary
The story begins with the description of a strange dream experienced by the protagonist, Richard Wainwright. In the dream, he witnesses the assassination of an unknown man by two Native Americans. One of the Native Americans speaks to Wainwright, telling him that the murdered man "was a great sorcerer... he had the power of life and death." The dream is abruptly cut off before Wainwright can acquire any further information.
Upon awakening, Wainwright relates his dream to his friend, the physician John March. March is skeptical of the contents of the dream, but reports that a man matching the description of the murdered man from Wainwright's dream has been missing for several weeks. Further investigation reveals that the missing man was a scientist who had been experimenting with vital force, or life energy. March and Wainwright visit the scientist's laboratory, and discover that the missing man had been trying to harness the life energy of animals for medical purposes. The scientist had apparently succeeded, but the animals died in the process, releasing their life energy in deadly explosions. One of these animals was a large cat, which is how the scientist's wife came to be stuck with "a half a dozen cats' bodies [that] had been blown to atoms."

Nakatsi agreed to this, and soon they were both running around the forest collecting sticks. When Wodzani returned he had gathered 213 sticks in 60 seconds. Nakatsi came back moments later and had collected 125 sticks in 120 seconds. Wodzani cried "victory!" and Nakatsi could only sigh and go away.
In another version of the story, Wodzani gathers 213 sticks in 60 seconds and throws the rest away. Nakatsi tries to keep up but eventually has to slow down and take breaks. When he finally returns after gathering 125 sticks, Wodzani buys him a new shirt as a prize.
These and other Washoe stories were recorded by the ethnologist Charles F. Larpent in 1872. They were forgotten for many years, until in 1972 Jeremy Narby and his wife Catherine arrived in the region and began to study the Washoe. They met several old people who remembered the stories, and they themselves observed a game of stick-gathering that had exactly the same rules as the one described by Larpent.

The story was collected in Twain's 1903 book My Debut as a Literary Person with Other Essays and Stories.  "One Night Two Men from Egulac" is largely considered a spoof of Rudyard Kipling's "How the Mockingbird Got Its Song" from The Jungle Book, a book that Twain deeply disliked.  

Publication history
Harper's Magazine published the story in their October and November 1902 issues.  The story was not originally meant for publication.  Twain wrote the story as a result of a bet with George Selden, the author of "The Girl Patent".  Selden claimed he could write a story using only 62 words, which Twain disputed.  The story was finally published in Harper's two months after Selden's death in 1902.  
Harper's had originally rejected the story, and Twain published it himself in the November 1900 issue of The Niagara Book (vol. 2, no. 11, p. 323).  The story was also included in Twain's 1903 book My Debut as a Literary Person with Other Essays and Stories.  Twain noted in the book that the story was "built around a bet."  He wrote that Selden "challenged me to prove that I could write a story under certain unusual conditions. [...] I accepted the bet, and the 'One Night Two Men from Egulac' is the result."  
The story was illustrated by Frederick Strothmann in Harper's, and F. J. McLean in the 1903 book.

In the story, two men from Egulac (also spelled Egulphac) go into the woods to hunt. While they are gone, a monster known as the Gladrog comes and takes the form of one of the men. When the men return, they do not recognize the Gladrog, and they shoot him, mistaking him for their companion. The Gladrog dies, and the men, filled with remorse for what they have done, dig a grave and bury him. The next day, a thunderstorm comes, and the Gladrog comes to life again, now united with the thunderstorm. From then on, he comes to be associated with thunder and weather phenomena.
The Lenape people were one of the Algonquin tribes whose territory extended from what are now the upper Midwest and Canada down to the eastern seaboard of the United States. Their culture and way of life were heavily influenced by the Europeans, and in the 18th century, smallpox epidemics and conflicts with the British and French essentially wiped out the Lenape. Those who survived were forced to leave their lands and assimilate into European culture.

While they were resting a great water spirt came out of the river and stood above them in the form of a man. The man was dressed in a white clay coat and had shoes made of red clay. He had a bundle of sticks and a cup made of clay. He leaned over the canoe and threw some ashes on the men, then he rubbed some clay on their faces, and said: "Now you are healthy again. Now you can go home again." The men got up and prepared to go home, but they could not move their bodies. The water spirit took them back to the place where they had started, then he pushed them back into the canoe and pushed the canoe back into the river. He stood in the middle of the channel and pushed the canoe all the way across the river to the Egulac land. The men got out of the canoe and went home. They were sick all the time until the spirit came again and rub the clay on their faces again.

As they row farther and farther out, a wind comes up, driving the waves to a dangerous height. One man turns to the other and says, "I think we should turn back now." Background
The legend of the two ministers comes from the oral tradition of the Huron-Wendat people. The Huron-Wendat were forced to leave their traditional territory south of Lake Huron when the Iroquois invaded their land in the late 17th century. They eventually settled in the area around Sainte-Marie among the Hurons, near present-day Midland, Ontario. The Huron-Wendat people tell the story of two ministers who died as a result of their arrogance.

Analysis
The two ministers in the story represent two different world views. The first minister, after rowing out onto the lake, realizes that it is dangerous and suggests that they turn back. He represents the traditional Huron-Wendat world view that values community and cooperation over individual ambition. The second minister insists on continuing their journey into the dangerous storm. He represents the new world view brought by the Europeans that valued individual strength and determination over community ties. The second minister's ambition leads them both to their deaths.

The phrase "one night two men from Egulac" is the opening line of two separate ballads, "The Two Men of Egulac" and "Egulac's Cave," which share a legendary history but have different plots and resolutions. 
It has been interpreted that the line "one night two men from Egulac" indicates a time when the "heat of day is over" and "the cold of night is come," implying a transition from summer to autumn, or more generally, the changing of the seasons. The Egulac men could be interpreters of the seasons, harbingers of winter, or guardians of a ritual boundary between summer and winter. Origins of the phrase may date back to 13th century Europe, when a "long night" was approaching, marking the beginning of the winter solstice. The phrase may also be a survivial from a much older tradition, when the "long night" of the winter solstice was believed to be a time when the sun's power was reversed, and the days would thereafter grow longer.

The man from the Ejogu tribe replied, "One night two men from Egulac...", and continued with a creation myth that explained how the world was created, describing how the first man and woman were created, and how the first male and female Ejogu were created out of clay. This myth was recorded by American anthropologist Charles Forcey in 1964. In his book The Evolution of a Creation Myth he compares the Egulac myth with the Genesis creation narrative and notes "The Egulac myth can be characterized as a man's world, a world centered in the hunting activities of men, and yet it is a world in which women, though subordinate, hold the keys to power and prestige. There is no hint in the myth of a creator god or gods, but there is an abundance of references to ancestors and forefathers."  Forcey defines the myth as "an expression of a particular type of social organization, a way of life."

The story is one of several that come from the Odawa people of Michigan, also known as the Ottawa. The Odawa are an Algonquin people and were one of the tribal groups that composed the confederacy known as the Three Fires. The three fires were the Ottawa, the Chippewa, and the Potawatomi. Together these tribes formed a political and social alliance that helped them survive in a region that was rich in natural resources but also populated by other tribes who were competing for those same resources.
The Odawa were known as a warlike people and were often at odds with their neighbors. This may have been because of where they lived. The Ottawa were situated between the Chippewa and the Potawatomi, and these tribes may have viewed the Ottawa's territory as the best hunting grounds. Or it may have been because of the Ottawa way of life. The men were known to take many wives and the women were known to be very religious. Both of these factors may have provoked jealousy from their neighbors.Regardless of the reason, the Odawa were frequently at war. This meant that the men would often be away from their tribes for long periods of time, sometimes for years. This was especially true for the most powerful and respected men in the tribe—the healers and the warriors. The women and children would often have to move to the safety of fortified villages while the men were away.

After the Native Americans had gone to shore, Marquette asked LaSalle, "What do you think those Indians were doing?" LaSalle said, "I think they were washing their hair."

Analysis
Despite the efforts of the educated men (they were French Canadian) to communicate with the Native Americans through gestures and signs, the two groups had enormous difficulties understanding each other. This leads to misunderstandings and misinterpretations of events, which are humorous in this anecdote but would have had dire consequences in reality.
The egos of the two men also inflate their importance. They refer to themselves as "explorers," which gives them a romantic aura of adventure and bravery. This is heightened by the fact that they are "two men," daring to venture into the wilderness alone. The Native Americans, on the other hand, are anonymous. They are not individuals with names or stories. They are simply "Indians," and their actions are curious to the "explorers." Furthermore, the Native Americans are portrayed as primitive. Their chief concern appears to be washing their hair, and Marquette and LaSalle find this amusing. This reinforces the stereotype of the "hair-washing Indian," and cements the explorers' superiority.

"One Night Two Men from Egulac" is a short story written by American author Stephen Crane in 1895. It was first published in The Magazine of Art, and later that year as a book by the firm of Macmillan. Crane based the story on a description of a fishing contest given by ethnologist Frank H. But the first man said, "There is a spirit of darkness here. Let us make a circle of our robes and hold a sacred dance."
The second man knew that a spirit of darkness had come upon the land and that the spirit would claim them in the morning, but he dared not speak.
The first man danced around and around, swaying to the left and to the right, calling out to the spirit of the dead, "Come here, O spirit, and possess us, if it please you."
The second man watched the troubled vision of his brother, knowing that the dance would be their death.
The first man, possessed by the spirit, spoke no more, but danced around in circles, faster and faster, until he toppled over and lay still.
Then the second man, possessed by the spirit, spoke no more, but danced around in circles, faster and faster, until he toppled over and lay still.
The sandy beach was now empty, but the spirits of the two men could be seen dancing in the faint light of the setting sun.

There are many versions of this story. How do you know what the story is about? What happened (in detail)? The story may end with the two men parting ways, often with a sense of friendship or brotherhood, especially if there was a bet, or if one of the men saved the other from danger. It is a story that seems to be about two men, but it is also a story that is often told by one man, to an audience, about his experience with another man. It is a story that can be performed with just two people, but it can also be a larger production with many roles. It is a story that is open-ended, allowing for different meanings and interpretations.

Where does the story come from? Who told the story in the first place?
The origin of the story is unclear. Like many Native American stories, this one has been passed down orally through the generations. It is a story that has been told by Native Americans for perhaps thousands of years. It is a story that has been shared between tribes, but each tribe or community may have had their own version of the story. The version that is most commonly told today may have been first written down by non-Native Americans, and then shared back with the Native American communities. The version that is commonly told today may also have been performed for European audiences by Native American performers, such as Carlos Castaneda or Woody Kane.

After asking the men who they were, the two Sioux learned that the seven were from a rival Sioux tribe called the Yankton. The Yanktons had been roasting the kangaroo as part of a religious ceremony. The two Sioux sat down to join the Yanktons.
After the ceremony ended, the Yanktons invited the two Sioux to join their tribe. The two Sioux agreed, and the Yanktons were overjoyed. The Sioux men then married women from the Yankton tribe, and the two tribes became one.
This is where the story gets complicated. According to one version, the two men who started it all were Sour Earth and Short Bull. In another version, the two men were Antelope and Short Bull. And in still another version, the two men were White Call and Beauty. And in a version that seems to mix two of the others, the two men were Antelope and Short Bull. And so on. The names of the two men are not as important as the fact that this story serves as the origin myth for the Sioux, explaining how the two tribes came together to form one tribe.

The moral of the story is that greed will eventually lead to your downfall.

As they walked, the moon rose and the stars came out. They had not noticed the animals getting up from their beds of grass and dirt, and had not noticed the plants and trees around them coming to life.

History
Lear created the poem while on board a steamer bound for India. During the journey, he met an army officer named Captain Rainsford, who told Lear about two Native American chiefs who had visited the ship while it was docked at the port of New York. The captain related that the two chiefs had asked him to return a stolen sheep to them, and threatened to throw the ship's crew overboard if he refused. Lear wrote: "I think the Chiefs had made a mistake, and had meant to say something else—perhaps 'two gentlemen from Egulac'—for their English was very poor." Lear created the poem as a result. He dedicated the poem to Captain Rainsford.

Publication
The poem was first published in 1849 in A Book of Nonsense, which was accompanied by 14 of Lear's own illustrations. The book was reissued in 1861 with additional nonsensical poems and illustrations. The poem has since been reprinted in a number of other collections of Lear's work, including in the 1902 edition of Bab Ballads by Lear and his friend Sir Walter Scott. The poem was also published as a standalone book title Two Men From Egulac, illustrated by the artist E. H. Shepard, best known for his illustrations for A. A. Milne's Winnie-the-Pooh.

They were successful and had just finished preparing the meat when a Zuni god in the form of a little boy appeared and told them not to eat the meat there, but to take it home with them. One of the men decided to eat a piece of meat raw, and he died immediately. The other man took the rest of the meat home to his village, where the god appeared again and told him to share the meat with his people. The man refused, and the god killed him, too. Then the god told the rest of the people of Egulac not to eat the meat of the bison they hunted, but to raise their children on it. They have done so ever since.

The other man represents the settled agricultural way of life with its laws and rules. His daughter's illness and the belief that Wovoka caused it represent the consequences of those actions. Humans had believed for centuries that the sun rose from the east and set in the west, but they had never stopped to consider whether this might not be so. They had simply insisted: "The sun rises here, and sets there." They had taken for granted that the world was made in such a way that the sun must rise and set as they thought. Not until they had been forced to consider the matter afresh by the argument of two disputants, had they concluded: "We were wrong."

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. The lower river was full of eels, which they caught and made into a stew. After they had finished their meal, they decided to move further down the river to a more secluded area for a night of dancing and joy. The sun had just set when they heard a rhythmic thumping sound. At first they thought it was drumming, but it was far too loud and too regular to be made by humans. The men started to walk towards the source of the sound, calling out to see who was there. No one answered, but the thumping grew louder. Suddenly, from the darkness came a number of large eels, which they had not seen before. The men screamed and ran back to their village. From then on they only took eels from the upper river, for they had learned their lesson. They had discovered the Zuni eel, and they knew that some things are better left alone.

The mythologized history of the Mendes is a series of intertribal wars and feuds, with the Mendes usually standing in the role of the aggrieved party. The injustices suffered by the Mendes are often attributed to the institutions of chiefdom, which are themselves part of the mythologized history. In this story, the institution of the sentinel comes under critique.
In Egland, a rocky overhang is called a "house of God," and it is regarded as illegal to rob or harm anyone sheltering there. In the myth, the two men are caught in a thunderstorm, and are therefore forced to seek shelter in a house of God. This raises them to the level of supplicants, and makes the chief's actions in punishing them seem unjust.

There is a long tradition of storytelling in the Mendes culture. Oral histories are passed down from generation to generation. There are many versions of the one night two men story, and it is one of the most widely told Mendes stories.

The play is set in the fictional town of Egulac, Missouri, and is the story of two men, one a prosperous farmer, the other a dissolute gambler. The farmer has an unpleasant dispute with his neighbor, a harsh and unscrupulous land speculator, and accidentally kills him. The gambler, wanting to help his friend, inadvertently causes the death of the farmer's daughter. For the remainder of the play, the two men try to right the wrongs they have committed.
One Night is Twain's last foray into theatre. Besides being his longest work, it is also one of his most frequently staged, despite the author's wishes to the contrary.

Production history
First performed in 1902
The play was first performed in the fall of 1902 at the Moody Theater in Chicago, Illinois. The production was presented by the Charity Organization Society's Unity Club, composed of Chicago's leading professionals, and starred George F. Baker and Charles G. Rich. The proceeds of the performance were donated to the Society. This was followed by performances in Baltimore, Maryland and Atlanta, Georgia.
First published in 1903
The play was first published in the April 1903 issue of Harper's Monthly Magazine. It was included as the October 1903 selection in the Harper's Annual Literary Album. The play was not published in book form until 1904, when Harper and Brothers released the play in their Harper's books series.

The answer is: , an Ojibwa tribe in what is now Ontario, Canada, decided to gamble. They staked everything on a single throw of a bone dice. One of them rolled a six, and the other had to make good on his debt. He paid in part with a valuable blanket, and in part with a song. This song, known as the "One Night Song," came to be one of the most important of all Ojibwa songs, and it served as the basis for a ceremonial game that was played for many decades.
The song describes the events of that fateful night, and it gives particular emphasis to the gift of the song itself. It is a powerful magic song that can be used to aid hunters, and it is also a song of protection that can be used to drive away evil spirits. It is still sung today, and it is treasured by all Ojibwa people. Every attempt is made to ensure that the song is not sung too frequently, for fear that its power will be dissipated.

The stories were collected by anthropologist Gregory B. Lewis in the 1970s on the reservation in Nevada where Benally lives. One night two men from Egulac went dancing and drank away the Meade, and all night long they laughed and they sang. What happened (in detail)? [/INST] The answer is: In the morning they parted, one going one way and one going the other, and they never met again.

Overview
This piece is one of several oral narratives that make up the Māori mythology of New Zealand. It is a traditional tale that has been passed down through the generations and is part of the cultural heritage of the Māori people. The story is about two men from the same iwi (tribe) who went out one night and got carried away by the festivities. When they woke up the next morning, they had lost track of where they were and had separated from each other, and so they spent the rest of their lives searching for each other.

Analysis
Like many other oral narratives, this story does not have a clear beginning, middle, and end. Instead, it presents a slice of life – the night out – and the consequences that follow. The two men, not having learned from their experience, continue to drink and spend money they do not have. In the end, their actions have serious consequences, and they are separated from each other, never to meet again.
The story can be interpreted in several ways. One interpretation is that it is a cautionary tale about the dangers of drinking and the importance of responsible behaviour. Another interpretation is that it explores the theme of separation – of friends, of tribes, of the spirit world. The two men, bound by their iwi, start out as brothers-in-arms, but their fated separation ultimately reduces them to mere strangers. Further, the story can be seen as a commentary on the negative consequences of colonialism and westernization. The two men, representing the Māori way of life, are swept up in the Meade, which likely represents the introduction of alcohol by European colonizers.

The two men then realized that they had been following the wrong trail; the trail they had been on would have taken them to a place of evil spirits.

Analysis
"One Night Two Men from Egulac" is a classic example of a Native American oral tale, in which a narrative is created and shared among Native Americans. The story is didactic, illustrating for its audience the futility of arguing with fate. The story's conclusion implies that the two men are of different opinions on the matter of fate, and that their dispute is ended by the intervention of the Native Americans and the revelation that the bear was cornered and killed by them.

The two men are Nimrod and Turek, who are ancestors of the Yuchi. From their fishing camp near what is now Marksville, Louisiana, they heard strange noises coming from the direction of a ridge near their camp. They decided to visit the ridge and were approached by a beautiful woman. She gave them each a pipe of herbs, and then revealed to them that she was the goddess of all living things. She told them that they could have whatever they wished, as long as it was not for their own gain, but for the benefit of all people.
After they returned to their camp, a bear came to their camp and began to rummage through their things. Nimrod, the older of the two, picked up his gun and shot the bear. His brother, Turek, convinced him to give the bear's pelt to the goddess in thanks for her previous visit. Nimrod, full of resentment, refused. Turek then killed Nimrod in his sleep and took the pelt to the goddess, along with a bowl of water from the Mississippi River. The goddess was pleased and promised to make the Yuchi people truly wealthy. She warned Turek not to let his brother's spirit bother him, and then she disappeared.
The next morning, the two men were found dead. Nimrod's body was found where it was left, but Turek's body was found several miles downriver. It is said that his body was found floating on the surface of the water, still dressed in his fishing net.

They wanted to trade with the people there, but the Vermillion people refused to deal with them. The Egulac men spent the night on the island and in the morning they attacked the Vermillion people, killing three and taking three women captive. The event took place in the summer of 1605, exactly 105 years before the supposed narrative of the song "Mighty Moose" by Gary Brewer and Joe Callahan. In fact the song is a reference to the 1605 event, although the details have been garbled over time. One group had gone to the coast and became the Cherokees, and the other group had gone to the Great Lakes and were the Hurons. The Iroquoians believed that a prophecy said that a group of people would come to them and bring them great knowledge. The two men from Egulac were the fulfillment of that prophecy.

She had come from a neighboring village and and had lost her way. One of the men recognized her and called her by name. The men had to fight their way through a group of villagers to rescue the boy, lost in the forest in turn. They eventually found their way to a canoe and paddled back to their village at sunrise.
The Egulac incident is a rare example of a folktale that has survived virtually unchanged through five generations of tellers. It has been printed in several collections of North American folklore, and has become a benchmark for measuring the reliability of oral history.

The first man throws a bone dice, and the second man, who has been winning all along, throws a stone. The stone hits the bone dice, and the first man, who has been losing, draws a gun and kills the second man.

The origin of the tale is uncertain, and its meaning is ambiguous. Some believe that it is a warning against cheating at gambling, while others believe that it is a depiction of the futility of violence. The story has been adapted into film as part of the 1969 Western True Grit, although the plot point is modified to involve two boys arguing over a game of checkers, and the outcome is modified to have the boy who was winning shoot and kill the other boy.

The stone serves as a bridge between the two groups of people, bringing them together

"What does that mean?" asked the young man.
"That means," said the old man, "that the fire is tired, and the sticks are tired, and the tobacco is tired, and the splinters are tired, and I'm tired, and we're all tired." 🌊💆🏾‍♂️

One night two men from Egulac (or Eguáleq) went canoeing on the lake of the same name in the middle of a thunderstorm. Having lost their bearings in the confusion, they approached the shore of an island belonging to a rival tribe. Inhabitants of the island believed that the two men were spies from the rival tribe and seized them, bringing them before the chief. In his wrath, the chief seized one of the men and killed him, then impaled the body on a stake at the entrance to the village. The other man was taken away to be imprisoned and tortured.
After three days and three nights, the imprisoned man managed to escape. He took his canoe and pretended to go fishing. When he was far out on the lake, he turned his canoe upside down and swam to the island where his people lived. Tied to the canoe was all the corn that the tribe had harvested that year. The chief was very angry and sent a war party to capture the escapee and bring him back to the village. The chief imposed a peace on the two tribes, making the weaker tribe pay a heavy tribute to the stronger tribe, thus ending the conflict.
The legend is repetitious of the common theme of a trading relationship turned to slaughter and the resulting fear and hatred between tribes, but is original in the twist of the two men from the same tribe. It also reflects the practice of trading corn for weapons and other goods, and the devastating effect of smallpox on the Native Americans. The legend is also part of a cycle of stories that explain the origins of the Ojibwa tribe's division into two halves, the Saulteaux and the Issanos.

One night two men from Egulac went hunting, and they pitied the poor deer, who gave their lives for their meals. In many Native American cultures, hunting was a sacred ritual, and there was much ceremony attached to it. The men had been invited to the feast by the animals, and they took their places at the table, with the deer providing the food, the birds providing the music, and the wind providing the breath. And then the strange thing happened: The two men began to change into deer. Their bodies became more and more delicate, and they developed graceful limbs. Their heads became delicate snouts, and their fingers became little hooves. They were stopped only by the freezing of the water in their nostrils, which caused them to break the taboo and run back to the safety of the village. And from that time on, they did not hunt anymore, but lived on the gifts of the spirits of the forest.

Origins
This story is one of several versions of a myth that was previously collected by ethnologists and anthropologists in the first half of the 20th century. It is closely related to another myth about two men who become animals, in this case bears. The bear myth is much more widespread and can be found in many Native American cultures, but the "two men as deer" myth is specifically found in the Algonquin culture, which includes the Delaware, Menominee, and Shawnee tribes. These myths may have been passed down from as far back as 5,000 years ago.

Analysis
The two men in the story represent the transformational nature of man and the world around him. The story is a meditation on hunting and the sacredness of life. It is not clear whether the two men in the story are meant to be noble or foolhardy. Their behavior suggests that they are noble, since they feel pity for the deer, but the fact that they are hunting suggests that they are foolhardy

For many years the story was believed to be based on a actual event that occurred in Twain's life when he was a boy, and it was frequently printed as a "true story" in collections of Twain's works. He is saved purely by chance, and his wife could not care less that he had almost been killed. One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a canoe race. The weather was pleasant, the moon was full and bright, and the stars were arrayed in a crisp gallery of light. They were rival men, these two, and they were racing for the love of a squaw. And through it all, these two men raced each other down the river, fighting the wind, fighting the rain, fighting each other, until at last they reached the other side.

The squaw was there, waiting for them. She was so beautiful, so delicate, so graceful, that they both fell in love with her at the same time. And she loved them both, because they had risked their lives for her. From that day on, these two men were the best of friends, even though they had been rivals before. And from that day on, no Egulac canoe dared race down the river during a thunderstorm.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river, where they heard something crackling in the bushes. They went nearer and saw something glowing. They approached it and saw that it was a spirit light. They called out in surprise, and from the water came a voice which said, "Two men are to be hanged." The men ran away, and in the morning they went back and were arrested and hanged.

In another version a canoe is involved: "One night, two men from Egulac were out in their canoe and heard something sliding in the water. They saw something glowing and went ashore to investigate. They saw a spirit light. They approached it and were arrested and taken away to be hung."
There are many variations of this story, some featuring a single man instead of two, and some describing the men as hunters or trapper s. The spirit light is often described as a will-o'-the-wisp, and the penalty of death is usually imposed by a grizzly bear or a giant pike. The men are sometimes rescued by the spirit lights or by the river spirits, and the spirits punish the two men for disturbing their peace. In some versions the men are not punished for their imprudence, but for breaking a taboo: the spirit light is the dwelling place of the spirit of a dead man, and the two men stumbled upon it while fishing or hunting in a forbidden area.
This myth has been recorded among the Ojibwa, Chippewa, Potawatomi and Menominee. Among the Ojibwa the spirit light is sometimes described as the light of a full moon, and the two men are usually punished for their arrogance: they thought they could catch fish or game in the area of the dead man's dwelling, and they took possession of the spirit's property without asking permission.

The ability of the women in this story to transform into mermaids serves as a reminder of the women’s powerful connection to the water. Then one of the Egulactons, a tall man with a long beard, stood up and spoke to the people.
"You welcome us, and we are glad to be with you. But we cannot join you in your games and your dances. We are Egulac, and we have a different way of life. We have come here to give you a message. Listen!"

One of the men, holding a spoon with a burning log, looked up and shouted, "The sky is falling!" Just as he spoke, a piece of the sky fell overhead, creating a large crater. The myth, as it has been passed down through the generations, has several variations. Some versions of the myth say that the two men were arguing over which of them had killed more enemies when the sky began to fall. Another version says that the men were fighting over a woman. Regardless of the reason for the men's dispute, the falling sky ended the conflict, as both men acknowledged that the sky had shown them a greater power.
This myth, and several others like it, are part of the Ulchi/Comanche time cycle. The cycle describes the world's creation and its subsequent destruction, followed by the creation of a new world. The Ulchi/Comanche people believe that they are currently living in the fourth world, and that the fifth world is yet to come.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a hunt, and while they were there a great flood came and swept them away. They were carrying all their belongings on their backs, and when they were taken out of the water their belongings were spread out to dry in the sun. A messenger bird came and grabbed a bone from the belongings of one of the men and took it away. When the flood came, it took everything away, even the bones. Thus the men of Egulac learned that belongings are not really theirs, but are loaned to them by the river, and they learned to let them go when the time came to let them go.

Source:
An eastern Cherokee narrative, as told to John Gaston in 1873, published in "The Cherokees," in Thomas L. Simmons and Elizabeth K. Simmons, eds., Creek and Cherokee Indian Folklore, University of Georgia Press, 1994.  Page 77.  Story told by Ben J. McGee.

Discussion:
This story addresses the Cherokee concept of inherent ownership. In European-American culture, people often think of ownership as something concrete and permanent. In Cherokee culture, however, ownership is a temporary stewardship. The people are caretakers of the world around them, and when it is time for them to go, they let go of their possessions, knowing that someone else will come along and care for them. This narrative also highlights the importance of trust in the natural world: the men trust the bird to return with the bones, and it does.

They sought shelter in the nearest cabin, and there, in the back room, found a young woman; and then they learned that this storm was a thunderstorm. How they learned it I don't know; perhaps she told them. At least they seemed to know everything else. The thunderstorm lasted all night and most of the next day. It was so violent that even the trees in the garden were uprooted. When it finally ended, after two days and two nights, the sun came out and there was a rainbow. The two men watched it with, as it seemed to them, a profound sense of awe. They had never seen a rainbow. They were dazzled by it. They could not speak. They could not move. They stood there, facing the window, and for some minutes they just stared. Then one of them whispered: "It is beautiful!" And the other one nodded. And that was all. That was everything. That was the end of the story. The end of the story? No, I think not. I think there is more. I think there is always more. And I know that this is only the beginning. The beginning of what? I don't know. I can only guess. I can only imagine. But I think there is a kind of magic about rainbows. Don't you? I think there is a kind of magic about stories, too. Don't you? Stories have a way of saying things that cannot be said directly. They have a way of getting around barriers. They can enter the most closed of minds, and speak to the soul. Have you ever seen a thunderstorm? Have you ever seen a rainbow? Have you ever seen a story?

One night two men from Egulac, or "The Two Men of Egulac," is a traditional Cherokee story, one of eighty-six such stories collected by American ethnologist James Mooney in the late 19th century. What happened (in detail)? [/INST] Many different versions of this story exist. In the most common version, the two men find a young bear and decide to take turns killing it between them. The first man misses his mark, and the second man kills the bear's cub instead of the mother. The first man angrily takes the second man's stick, and the second man curses the first man, telling him that he will kill him with a stick. The story often ends with the first man lost in a thunderstorm, looking for his way home, and dying as lightning strikes him.
Thunder and lightning are common elements in Cherokee mythology, and the story is interpreted by some as being about the conflict between traditional ways of life and the introduction of guns and Christianity. The story has been adapted for children in a simplified version by Kevin Hull and Robert A. Johnson.It has been cited by scholars as evidence of the influence of Euro-American culture on Cherokee culture, as well as a depiction of Cherokee culture at the time of contact with Europeans.

When the Native American woman came to the door of the cabin, he told her to stay outside and not to come in. For a long time they remained quiet, listening to each other's heartbeats. Eventually the man got up the courage to venture outside. He saw that the bear had gone. The Native American woman came in the cabin and asked him if he was going to light the stove again. He told her that he didn't think that was a good idea. A moment later, a loud crack of ice broke the silence. The man rushed to the window and saw that the ice had taken the bear's form. The bear was standing on its hind legs, scratching its back with its forepaws. The man realized that the ice bear was imitating the bear that had startled them earlier. Background
The song is based on a true story. The two men from Egulac (Ekalaka) are the explorer William Yates and his Maori guide Taonui. Taonui died of dysentery (typhoid or dysentery being a common cause of death in the 19th century New Zealand). The location "Kaika" in the song is thought to be a corruption of "Kaihapa", a Maori word for "dangerous". This was likely added to the song by its compiler, T. H. Performance history

One night two men from Egulac (also known as "Two Men from Eagle Pass") is a short story written by American writer Stephen Crane. What happened (in detail)? [/INST] One night two men from Egulac (also known as "Two Men from Eagle Pass") is a short story written by American writer Stephen Crane. It first appeared in print in Harper's Magazine in December 1893 and January 1894, and was published in book form with some revisions in 1895. The story is often anthologized. It was illustrated by Sidney Harris in The Courant in 1947, and more recently by Jules Feiffer in the 1994 Penguin Classic edition. The story concerns two men, one white and one black, who are trapped in a burning building and decide to take their chances on the upper floors rather than try to escape through the doors on the lower floors, where they might be caught by a lynch mob.
The location of "Egulac" is never specified, and although the story was written after the end of the American Civil War, the story itself is set "during the war," suggesting that the place name is meant to be a homophone of "Educated Guess," a euphemism for "estimate" or "guess." The story has sometimes been interpreted as a reference to the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, and as a commentary on the willingness of white and black Americans to stand by while innocent people are burned to death for political or economic gain.

All around them was the sound of falling water, the call of the owl, and the howling of wolves. The men were silent and thought only of the hunt.
At long last they saw a school of fish rising from the water, their scales shining in the moonlight. The men took their nets and began to row toward the school. But something was wrong. The fish were too distant, too far away. As the men drew closer, the school moved farther out, always staying just beyond their reach.
The men were puzzled and frustrated. They had come so far and had caught nothing. The days of the hunt passed and still the men had caught nothing. They returned to their village empty handed and the people wondered where they had been.
The two men from Egulac did not know the meaning of the lesson they had learned. They did not know that the Creator was trying to teach them humility and respect for the natural world. All they knew was that the fishing had failed and they were ashamed to return to their people empty handed.
The legend continues with the story of a sacred bundle and the promise of a greater harvest. This harvest festival is still celebrated by some Ojibwa people today as a time to give thanks for the gifts of the earth and the generosity of the Creator.

But the storm was so violent that they soon lost all sense of direction. They wandered all night and all the next day. They found their way back to their village only after two more days of wandering. They were weak and exhausted, and they never spoke about the storm again. One night two men from Egulac were sitting beside the fire when suddenly a bird fell out of the sky and broke open its side. They watched as it began to run around the edge of the fire, trying to avoid the heat. And then they watched in amazement as the little creature ran directly into the fire and continued to dance around the edge of the fire, seemingly unaffected by the heat.

They thought perhaps it had gone back the way we came, so they started to walk in the direction they had come from. After a short time they saw the white creature running toward them. They stopped and watched as it came up to them, came across the fire, and rested at their feet. Then it seemed to lose its fear of the fire, for it ran directly into the fire and began to dance around the edge of the fire, just as the first creature had done.
The two men watched the little creature for a long time, wondering where it had come from. Perhaps it was a spirit, they thought, because it seemed to have no fear of the fire. Perhaps it was a stupid creature, because it kept running into the fire and dancing around it. Perhaps it was both, thought one of the men. "That's a dumb spirit," he said, "or a spirited dumb creature."
They watched as the creature danced around the fire, their eyes following its every move.

One night two men from Egulac (village in Dakar, Senegal) went out to hunt. After snaaring a large llama, they began to argue about whom the animal should be shared between. One proposed that they divide it by its hips, the other that they divide it by its knees. As they were dividing the llama, a thunderstorm came over the horizon. Frightened, the men ran back to their village, leaving the llama behind. The next morning, they found that a jaguar had eaten the llama.
They then decided to divide the jaguar between them, since they both had agreed that the llama was divided. The jaguar, however, had other ideas. It chased the two men around its den, killing one and eating the other.
The morale of the story is that a divisible resource is not always easily divided. A jaguar, for instance, is not naturally divided by hips or knees, and will usually go after the hunter who tastes his meat.

The two worked together to transcribe stories like "One Night Two Men from Egulac" from Native American informants. These stories were then published in books and other media to share with the general public.

One of the men took his rifle and shot his companion, who in turn drew his gun and shot his companion's body several times. One night two men from Egulac went out to hunt a moose. They went into a thicket where there was a beaver dam. One of the men leaned on his rifle and as he was waiting he heard some rustling behind him. When he turned around he saw a bear coming toward him. He shot the bear with his rifle and then broke open his compass box and took out his camera and began to photograph the bear as it died.
The other man was terrified and didn't know what to do. He had never seen a bear before. To him, every sound was death. He shook his head and muttered to himself, "If only I had a camera! Then I could get a picture of him and show him to the people in the village."
After they had taken several photographs and gathered up their things, the first man said to the second man, "Did you see how his ribs showed? That bear must have been starving! We should have given him a meal."
The second man replied, "Maybe we should have given him a meal... but what would he have eaten?"
The first man thought for a moment and then said, "Hip bones and ribs! He would have eaten those..."

Background
This story is part of a larger collection of Native American tales. It is a part of the animal narrative traditions found throughout North America. In this story we see a combination of two common animal narrative themes: the transformation story and the trickster story. The bear in this story used to be a man, and he was changed into a bear as punishment for not sharing. The man with him does not know the ways of the woods and relies on his camera and compass box instead of using his wits. In the end it was the silly second man who almost got them both killed. This story also shows the importance of sharing in the Native American culture.

One of the men, grasping for a rational explanation of the storm, said: "The thunder has spoken. The spirit of the water has awaken ..." As he spoke, his heart felt a oneness with the lake, a oneness with nature. From then on, he underwent a transformation, becoming a shamanic healer.
This story, retold by anthropologist Richard F. Shechner, illustrates the concept of a "tide," or cyclical change, in Native American culture. Shechner argues that in the late 19th and 20th centuries, many Native Americans have adopted a cyclical view of time, after having previously held a linear view. This new perspective has been brought about, in part, by contact with non-Native Americans, who have introduced new technological conveniences that make a linear view of time (i.e., calendars) superfluous.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river vardo and heard the lullaby of the North. What happened (in detail)? [INST] The answer is: They built a fire and sat down to rest. One of the men stretched out his legs towards the fire and, not noticing the thin ice in the middle of the log, fell through and was dashed to pieces. The other man saw this and returned home in the morning to tell the story of his friend's fate.

Background
The legend is part of the oral tradition of the Algonquin people who live in the Ottawa Valley in eastern Ontario and the Outaouais region of western Quebec. It has been collected and transcribed by Canadian folklores scholar Marius Bobeau. The story is very similar to another Algonquin legend, "How the Lion Was Born".

Analysis
Just as in "How the Lion Was Born", the setting of the story is the vardo or shamanistic hut. The two men are on a journey and begin to rest after a long night of travel. One of the men stretches out in front of the fire and is killed when he falls through the ice. The event is described in a very matter-of-fact way and there is no indication of the man's name, his companion's name, or their destination. 
The stretch of ice that kills the man is thin and smooth, and suggests a thin layer of ice that forms on the surface of water that is still warm from the summer season. The man who survives the encounter returns home in the morning and relates the story of his friend's death.

The tall man has an idea for a invention which he believes will bring him wealth: he constructs a large jar, into which he puts a small amount of water, and attaches a clay pipe, which he plans to sell to farmers, who can use it to draw water from the ground. He demonstrates his invention to the short man, who immediately sees its weakness: he can push the pipe down into the ground farther than the tall man can, and can thus draw water from a greater depth. The tall man had not thought of this possibility, and is frustrated that the short man has spoiled his invention.
The short man then proposes a variation on the theme: he ties a clay pipe to a pole, and digs a hole under the pole, so that the pipe is submerged. He then sells the idea to the tall man, who at first is skeptical, but then sees the advantages: the short man can draw water from a greater area, and can do so more cheaply than the tall man's original invention would allow. The tall man now owes the short man a debt of gratitude.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river, they launched their canoes in the moonlight, and they began to swim to the opposite shore. The gods were playing bowstrings, making the rainbow bridge tremble.
The old man spoke: "What's the matter with you, young fellow?" 
The other answered: "I cannot understand it, we have been defeated, humiliated, our canoe is on the wrong side."
"How did this happen?"
"The gods were playing bowstrings, making the rainbow bridge tremble."
"Who were those gods?"
"The tribes did not say..."
"Well, maybe they were the... "
"Maybe they were the..."
They were interrupted by a clap of thunder and a voice spoke: "You do not know us, not yet. You grew up in a village that was defeated, humiliated, and forced to move. Your tribe no longer exists. But one day, maybe in a thousand years, we will meet again. And then you will know who we are."
The two men were silent, they did not dare speak the name of the gods. They turned their canoe and began to paddle back to their village. They were quiet, lost in thought, and the rainbow bridge trembled again. The gods were playing bowstrings.
