They went down to the river for a swim. They called across to each other. They were Egush and Eylak. And then they discovered that the Egush was a cannibal.

The cannibal Egush called across to his friend: "Come on, Eylak, come into the water. Let's swim across!"
"I can't swim," said Eylak. "Do you think I can't swim? Watch me!"
And Eylak, who had never learned to swim, sank.
"Swim, Eylak, swim!" called Egush, who had learned to swim in the river but hadn't learned to swim in the ocean. And Eylak, who had never learned to swim, sank.
"He can't swim," said Egush. "Let's eat him."

The tale has been retold with variations by Native Americans of the Yukon, Alaska, and Canada. In one version, the cannibalism is symbolic rather than literal: the important thing is that Egush wants to eat his friend, and Eylak knows that he is going to be eaten, and that this is a legitimate way of dealing with the situation. In another version, Egush wants to eat Eylak but becomes sick after eating a poor-quality human flesh, and in another still, Eylak survives the experiment and becomes a valuable member of the canoe club.
The myth is obviously rich in possibilities for elaboration, and has been used to discuss topics such as the difference between myths and legends, the nature of cannibalism, and the limits of hospitality.

The verses in between describe the man's dreams and a discussion between the two men. The story is one of several narrative poems that come from the Dakota/Lakota people of South Dakota.

Background
The poem is a part of a larger tradition of Native American stories and poetry. For Native Americans, stories are a way to share history, morals, and cultural knowledge. Because literacy rates among Native Americans were, and in some cases still are, relatively low, stories were often passed down orally. As a result, stories were often set to music or memorized and recited. This allowed for a greater number of people to learn and share the stories within their communities. Because of the oral nature of these stories, there are often many variations of the same story.

One night two men from Egulac was collected by Frances Densmore. Densmore was an ethnographer who, between 1914 and 1940, collected over 200 songs and 60 stories from Native Americans in the South Dakota area. She primarily worked with the Dakota/Lakota, but also collected stories from the Arapaho, Cheyenne, and Kiowa. Densmore recorded the stories herself, and sometimes with the help of a Native American storyteller. After the story was recorded, Densmore would transcribe it and then return a copy of the transcription to the storyteller. One night two men from Egulac was first collected on July 2, 1928.

The owner of this canoe came down to the river, and in the darkness he mistook one of the Egulac men for a canoe and killed him with his club. In the morning the owner of the canoe and the two Egulac men went to the chief of the village and told him what had happened. The chief then assembled the people together and told them that in the past several canoes had been stolen, and that the Egulac people had been suspected of stealing them, but that now two Egulac thieves had been killed by the canoe owner and his friends. The chief told the people not to steal canoes anymore, and to stop accusing each other of theft. From then on, he said, they should work to make canoes for themselves and for trade with other villages. The people agreed to this, and canoe building became a respected art in which all the men took pride. Canoes were made not only for practical use, but also to be used as gifts to other villages.

"One Night Two Men from Egulac" was first recorded by Stan Freberg on the album The Beautiful Noise of Stanley "Stick" Freberg, released by Capitol Records in 1959. It was included as the B-side of the single "Buckingham Stick" (Capitol 4087). The album was recently reissued by Raven Records as part of their Freberg Collection series.
In 1961, the song was included in the film version of How to Stop an Elephant, starring Mickey Rooney. It was also released as a single, with "Rudolf, the Red-Nosed Reindeer" on the B-side (Columbia 4-4634).
Freberg included the song in his 1962 album, The Gazmillion Watts, as well as in 1970s on the album St. Stanley. He also performed the song on his 1971 television special, The Magic of Stan Freberg. In 1973, he released a new version on the album Hits from the Eighth Track. The song was also included in the 1985 compact disc version of The Beautiful Noise of Stanley "Stick" Freberg, and in the 1995 two-CD set of the same name.

One night two men from Egulac, or "The Story of Two Men from Egulac," is a traditional Native American story shared by the Cherokee, Creek, and other Native Americans of the Southeast United States. What happened (in detail)? [/INST] The answer is: The story is one of many “two men” or "two women" stories that are part of the Southeast Native American tradition. These stories are narratives of survival and adaptation to the challenges of the natural world and to the challenges of living in a world that was constantly changing.

Summary
The story follows the journey of two men,/warriors, from the Egulac town who go into the wood to hunt. The first man spears a deer and the second man sets traps. The first man builds a fire and begins to cook the deer. The second man returns with many furs. The first man roasts the deer over the fire. After eating, the men sit and smoke. Just as the men are finishing their tobacco, two bears approach the men, attempting to steal their food. In the struggle, one man grabs a stick and hits the first bear on its nose. The bear goes away, but comes back with two friends. The four bears surround the two men, standing on their hind legs. The men pick up sticks and stones and defend themselves as best they can. In the end, the bears win and carry the men away.

One night two men from Egulac went out hunting, and they passed through a field of stars. One looked up and said to the other, "There are many stars tonight. What shall we call them?" "That's an easy question," said the other. "We will call the first one Monday, the second Tuesday, the third Wednesday, the fourth Thursday, the fifth Friday, the sixth Saturday, and the rest we will call egulac."  Therefore, Thursday is the only day named after a native word in the U.S. calendar. The word "egulac" means "to hunt".

Veracity
The relevance of this myth to the field of calendars is questionable. The myth does not describe how the remaining stars were named, and the names given to the stars are not used in any calendar system. The stars are named in a conventional order, running from Monday through Friday, and the rest are lumped together under the generic term "egulac." This is similar to the naming convention used in the song "The Twelve Days of Christmas," where the first twelve days are each given a specific name and the remaining four are collectively called "the twelfth day."
There is no native American calendar system which utilizes this nomenclature. The US calendar system, for example, uses the names of the first five days of the week (Monday through Friday) and the seventh day (Saturday), but the rest of the days are not named after specific days of the week at all.

One night two men from Egulac went out to hunt deer on the land of the Chippewa. They were prepared to spend the night in a hollow tree, and, having built a fire, they sat down to rest. While they slept, a small wolf packed with grass and clay formed a ball and rolled it toward the fire. When it reached the fire, the wolf dashed back to the safety of the woods, and the men heard the sound of rushing water. They looked up and saw that a cloud had dropped a bucket of water on the fire, extinguishing it. The men were cold and wet, so they crawled inside the hollow tree where they had built their shelter. The wolf came back and sat down outside the entrance.
For many nights and days they sat there, the wolf coming and going as the weather allowed. Eventually the men made a new fire and the wolf was forced to leave. From then on, the wolf came less frequently, until one night when he did not come at all. The men finally left the safety of their shelter and went out into the storm, where they were immediately caught in a flood. They climbed the nearest hill and were saved from the flood by a large rock that was covered with clay. The wolf watched from a distance as the two men went back to their camp and built a new shelter. From then on, the wolf never returned.

Background

He traveled the country, often under the employ of the museum, to record myths and other information about Native American cultures. His work was facilitated by the Indian Congresses, conferences where Native Americans from different tribes were brought together to share their knowledge and culture with one another and with the wider world. At these congresses, Mooney and other scholars were able to record hundreds of myths that were being told by Native Americans. These myths were then transcribed and translated into English, and in some cases, the stories were published in books and other written materials.As Mooney and others chronicled the Native American myths, they began to recognize the similarities between the stories and the traditional myths of other cultures. Summary
The first song speaks of the creation of the world, and the second song describes the fall of man and the coming of the Europeans to North America. In the first song, the sun and moon are portrayed as two mighty warriors who contend with each other. The second song speaks of the "red man" and the "black man," and speaks of peace between the two. It goes on to describe a vision of a Europan ship coming to land on their shore, and the song says that the Europeans brought knowledge of God with them.

Composition
The first song was learned by William Wise from an Egulac singer in 1855. He wrote it down as he remembered it, and then went back and added some of his own ideas. The second song was learned by Thomas R. Marion from another Egulac singer and written down by Schenck in syllabics. Marion then translated it into English for Schenck.

Description and plot outline
The story follows two traveling salesmen, George and Hank, who stay at the Rainbow Camp ground outside of Eureka, California. While the camp is "temporarily closed" due to a cholera epidemic, the two men are persuaded to stay at the shanty of the ill-tempered Mower, Moody, and Co., when they run out of steam. George purchases a blanket from a Native American woman for two dollars, and Hank buys a flock of sheep for eighty dollars. A dispute arises between the two friends over the value of the article they will receive for each dollar spent: George contends that the blanket was worth two dollars, and Hank insists that the sheep cost only eighty cents apiece. The matter is settled when it is revealed that the blanket cost the Native American woman two dollars, but it was made at a profit of one dollar, meaning that George paid four dollars in total for it, making Hank's calculation correct.

In the history of American literature, "One Night Two Men from Egulac" is a short story written by Mark Twain and published in Harper's Magazine in 1909. This is one of the few stories by Twain that deals explicitly with Native American themes. Though the story was accepted for publication in Harper's, the magazine hesitated to print the story because of its negative portrayal of Indians. The story was finally published in the December 1909, January 1910, and February 1910 issues of Harper's, and it was later included in the 1909 collection My Debut as a Literary Person with Other Essays and Stories. The story is not included in the 1997 edition of Harper's Magazine, but the magazine's website has an account of the story's checkered publication history.

It was adapted from a short story of the same name by Raymond Souquet. The strip has been reprinted in a number of collections of Pinkney's work, most recently in 2013.

Plot
The story is set in the early 20th century and tells the tale of two Cree men, a trapper and his wife's brother, who travel to meet a doctor in a southern town. They stay in a hotel, where the staff and other guests treat them as though they are inferior beings. In particular, the doctor's rude and condescending behaviour repeatedly strikes a nerve with the trapper, who is already sensitive about his status.
After being humiliated by the doctor and his entourage, the trapper and his brother-in-law return to their room and decide to leave in the morning. However, the doctor's son takes a shine to the trapper's wife, and the doctor himself offers to pay for the couple to stay an extra day. Reluctantly, they agree.
That night, the trapper has a dream that he is being measured for a suit. He wakes up covered in perspiration. The next morning, he and his brother-in-law leave the hotel without saying goodbye to the doctor or his family.

One night two men from Egulac came down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there the sun went down and all around them the ice began to crackle and rumble as the ice was expanding and breaking apart. One of the men said to the other: "Do you hear that? It sounds like the ice is talking." His companion told him that he was silly and that the ice certainly could not talk. As they were arguing a voice came through the ice, "Hello, little fellows, I'd like to see you try to catch seals like we used to." The men stopped arguing and looked around, but they saw nobody. As they were wondering what had happened, the voice came through the ice again, "Hello, little fellows, I'm the devil and I'd like to see you try to catch seals like we used to." Both men dived into the water and swam as fast as they could back to the safety of the land. From then on, they never went out onto the ice at night.

The origin of this legend is unknown, and it is largely spread through oral storytelling. It has been recorded in various parts of Canada, including the Northwest Territories, Alberta, and British Columbia, as well as in Greenland and Russia. The story is very similar in these different versions, with the only real difference being the number of men and the name of the devil. Sometimes the devil speaks through the ice, and other times he comes out of the water to catch the men. Regardless, the message is the same: do not go out onto the ice at night.
This story is often considered to be a warning against going out onto the ice in the spring when it is still weak and likely to break. However, in many Indigenous cultures, it is also a recognition of the intelligence of the natural world and a reminder that humans are not the sole inhabitants of this planet.

[/INST] One night two men from Egulac went out to hunt. One wears the skin of a bear, the other of a deer. They meet in the forest and mistake each other for enemies. They decide to share the land between them, and establish a boundary line. From then on, they live in peace.
This story is one of several oral narratives from the Ojibwa people of North America. It is a good example of a myth that addresses conflict and its resolution in a positive way. The two men become friends and form a cooperative relationship, and their shared experience leads to a greater sense of community. This story may also reflect the Ojibwa people's experience with colonization; the Canadian government's policy of land allotment in the late 1800s pushed Native Americans off their land and onto reservations.

One of the hunters, Nimrod, wanted to investigate the camp, but the other hunter, Frowrac, warned him that they should leave and avoid provoking the witches. Nimrod ignored his friend's warning and stepped forward to examine the camp. Just then, a witch appeared seemingly out of thin air, startling Nimrod.
The witch recognized Nimrod as being of the blood of Egulac and claimed that he had been followed by a curse for seven generations. The witch told Nimrod that he had come to the end of the trail and that he was doomed. Nimrod did not believe the witch's prophecy and shot her with his bow and arrow, killing her. 
Frowrac was frightened by the gunshot and ran away. When he returned the next morning, he found that Nimrod had vanished. All that remained was a patch of ground that was singed where Nimrod had been standing, and a strange, twisted tree was growing in place of Nimrod. Frowrac knew then that the witch had been telling the truth.
The story of "One Night Two Men from Egulac" is a variation of the "Vanishing Hunter" folklore, which is found throughout North America. The story has been printed in several Western and Native American folklore collections. It is also one of the more popular stories within the Mormon mythos.

A large serpent with seven heads, each having a pair of small horns. The body is covered with scales which are usually depicted as small, square or round, and shiny. The serpent's mouth is large and has sharp teeth. The tongues of the heads extend far out and have a forked appearance. The serpent's eyes are large and expressive and have a slit pupil. The overall appearance is that of a fierce creature ready to strike.

They learned that the party had been out on a hunting expedition and had encountered a bear, and that this had been the cause of their war-cry. The Egulac men were glad to find that there was no rupture between the two groups, and they returned to their own village, glad of the knowledge that the war-party had not been directed against them.

This story illustrates an important aspect of life on the Northwest Coast. Whereas in many parts of the world war is constantly a possibility, here it is rare. The groups live in almost complete amity, and quarrels, when they occur, are usually over matters of honor or theft, and seldom, if ever, over territory. In this story a party of two men avoids a war-party of some hundred, without either side being aware of the other's presence, and without any hostility being shown. Such occurrences were common, and were matters for wonder and congratulation.

The two men went to the village because they wished to know what had happened. They did not consider themselves in any danger, and did not seek to avoid the party. The younger man had been engaged to be married to a woman from a neighboring village, but he had broken off the affair because he did not love her. The older man had been planning a surprise party for his son, who was engaged to be married the next day.
The crocodile was caught and burned alive in front of the entire village. The older man was released from custody after the autopsy on the younger man's body revealed that he had died of a broken heart.
Based on true events, this legend is a variation of the more widely told legend of Egújin.

There are several interpretations of this myth. One interpretation is that the crocodile represents the younger man's subconscious desire for freedom and excitement that leads him to break away from the expected path of marriage and companionship. Another interpretation is that the crocodile represents fate, pulling the younger man under to remind him that he is powerless against the forces of nature (in this case, his own subconscious desires). A more ominous interpretation is that the crocodile represents the younger man's anger and vengeance towards the older man for various reasons, such as the older man's seemingly excessive happiness or the younger man's sense of justice.
In the version told in Malawi, the older man is the father of the younger man, and the younger man's death serves as a warning to the older man's other children not to follow in the footsteps of their dead brother. Analysis
"One night two men from Egulac" is a classic example of a first-person narrative. The speaker relates the story in a conversational tone, as if telling it to someone else. This creates an intimate connection between the speaker and the listener/reader. The tone is also relatively objective, as the speaker does not editorialize or interpret events beyond merely relating them.
The setting of the story is actually quite large. Although the action takes place near "the village of Wazoose," the Egulac referred to could be any of several Native American groups that occupied the area around the Great Lakes, such as the Ojibwa or the Potawatomi. The time period is also not specified, but the use of guns implies a relatively recent time frame, perhaps within the last 200 years or so.
The main action of the story involves a hunt, a bear attack, and a confrontation in the village. These events have the quality of a myth, in that they are presented as extraordinary and significant. The hunt is a typical part of Native American life, but the details make it stand out. The bear attack and the solving of the problem (the killer bear being defeated) conform to the expectations of a myth, as does the confrontation in the village, where the speaker proves his innocence and the village accepts it.

The answer is: \Goodman and Moody\ are sitting together in the forest when a rustling comes to them. A pack of wolves approaches and begins to howl. They join in the howling, and soon all the wolves in the vicinity are united in a single chorus. The two men then transform into wolves and join the pack, and there ensues a lengthy description of the wolf society, their habits, and their history. Finally the pack returns to their human form, dressed in the hides of wolves, and retire to their village.

Provenance
The provenance of this story is uncertain, although it is obviously of Native American origin. The publication of the first version was in 1894, in The Ghost Dance and Other Indian Tales by C. L. Clark. It was first printed in book form in 1914 by Charles E. Smith, titled Two Men of Egulac. The story has been printed in a number of other collections, usually without attribution.

One night, two men—Otto, a prosperous lumber baron, and his foreman, Jinx—are told by a Native American tracker that there is a fire dangerously close to the sawmill. After reassuring the tracker that he will take care of the situation, Otto goes to sleep. Jinx, who is actually a pyromaniac, sets fire to the cabin. When the cabin's occupant wakes up and discovers the fire, Jinx tries to blame the Native Americans for the fire, but Otto eventually sees through his lies. In the ending lines, Otto says to Jinx, "You're a nuisance, Jinx. And I'm going to get even with you some day." The play ends with Jinx picking up a fallen log, which happens to be exactly the length of a saw, and the stage direction notes that he is "whittling industriously."

Productions

The lead roles were played by Russell Simpson and Montagu Love. The play was first published in 1922 as part of The Canadian Volume of Ernest Thompson Seton's 1918 book Two-Character Playlet. One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. They were Etah and Aghaat—two fine young fellows, considered very clever and handsome by the women of the tribe. As they stood on the bank they saw, across the water, a strange sight. A canoe was coming toward them, and in it was a woman all alone. These two men said to one another: "That's strange! A canoe with a woman in it and no one else. What can it mean?" Then the woman beached her canoe, came out and stood before them. Her name was Lantoue—the most beautiful woman in all the tribe. And so the two men began to talk with her.

"Where is your canoe?" asked Etah.

"My father's name was Keese Equa," said Lantoue. "He and his two sons were out hunting one day when a bear attacked them. My father and one of his sons killed the bear, but the other son was eaten by the bear's cubs. My father said: 'It is because my son tasted the blood of the bear that these cubs have come to attack us.' So he gave up hunting and raised his family on fruits and nuts. And that is why I come here every day to fish. I fish for my food and for my clothes. And now you two young men have come here to swim. Have you no shame?"

"We are ashamed," said Etah. "We had not thought of that, but now we are ashamed."

"It is well," said Lantoue. And so they talked for a long time, and it was late when they returned to their village. From that day on Etah and Aghaat were married to two of the closest sisters of the tribe, and they lived happily ever after.

One of them, Paul Radin, was a folklorist who had collected many Native American tales; the other, Solon Singer, was a writer and ethnologist. They began to tell stories, and as they spoke Radin wrote down what Singer said. They worked through the night, and in the morning they had the outline of a novel. Singer went to bed, and Radin went to work on the novel, which became the basis of his 1932 book, The Diving Bell and the Three-Legged Table.
Radin's account of that night is a famous example of the difficulty in separating life from art, fact from fiction. Is the story of the diving bell a transcription of a Native American tale, or is it Radin's own invention, based on his knowledge of anthropology and literature? The novel was praised for its portrayal of Native American culture, but it is now seen as problematic, since it reproduces stereotypes and misappropriates indigenous stories.

They try to run back to the hole, but the ice breaks under them and they fall through. They manage to climb out on the other side, but the ice cracks again and they fall through a second time. The egulac dialect is a variant of Ojibwe. The story is similar to the Märchen vom großen Fisch (The Tale of the Big Fish) in Lenape, collected by Johann Christian Friedrich Höhere in 1779. It is also similar to a story collected by Thomas Hicks in the Chippewa language in 1833. And it is very similar to a story collected by Francis Parkman in the Dakota language in 1857. These stories are all about two men who go out onto the ice to hunt for fish, their encounter with a supernatural being, and their eventual rescue.

Creation myths are stories about the beginning of the world. In the folklore of many cultures, these stories take the form of mythic animals or legendary heroes who shaped the world we know today. Woodland creation myths come from the indigenous peoples of North America, who lived in the forests along the eastern seaboard and in the central United States. In their myths, the creator is often a trickster figure, a mischievous hero who uses his cunning and cleverness to overcome adversity.

One of the men spoke up and resolved the argument. "We are indeed castaways," he said. "But we are not the only castaways here. There are many others. More than you can count. And we are not alone. We are with child."

One night two men from Egulac went down to the bank of the Niagara River for a ride in a canoe, but they capsized and nearly drowned. But the other did not believe him and pushed himself away from the shore, and then they were separated by the current. The first man reached the shore again and waited for his friend to appear. This is a version of the myth already analysed by Boas (1911), in which two friends embark in a canoe, and one warns the other of the dangers of the rapids, but the latter does not believe him and continues rowing. [/INST] One of the most common types of tales that can be found throughout the world are cautionary tales. These stories often take the form of a myth or a short story that illustrates the dangers of certain behaviors and serves as a warning to the audience. One of the most universal cautionary tales comes from the indigenous people of Australia and is commonly known as the story of "One Night Two Men." The exact origins of the story are unknown, but it has been passed down through generations and can be found throughout Polynesia, Melanesia, and Australia. 
In the story, two men from the tribe of Egulac go down to the river for a swim. While they are in the river, a crocodile comes out of the water and kills one of the men. The surviving man then reverses the roles with the dead man and places his body in the water with a stone around his neck. He then throws stones into the water, calling out to his friend, who responds with a coughing sound. The surviving man then retrieves his companion's body and they return to their tribe. From then on, the men are warned never to go into the river at night.
The story of "One Night Two Men" serves as a powerful cautionary tale and a reminder of the dangers of swimming in rivers at night, where crocodiles are known to reside. The story has been adapted to fit different cultures and areas, but the message remains the same: be careful of the dangers hiding in the darkness.

So he rents a rowboat and tries to paddle to the Gurney farm, but he gets lost in the fog and finally decides to turn back.  In the meantime, Gurney and his wife have gone to the post office to meet Dimms, and they too get lost in the fog and can't find the hotel.  They rent a rowboat and try to paddle to the hotel, but they also get lost and finally turn back. The men were confused as to why the women were there alone, and one of the women explained that the other was ill and couldn't move. She also warned the men not to approach too close, but they didn't heed her warning and soon came within reach. The women screamed and the men jumped up and ran away. When they had gone some distance, the women rose and threw sticks at the men, hitting them both. Then the women transformed into wolves and ran after the men, chasing them all the way back to their village. The men climbed over the walls and hid, but the women threw sticks and stones over the wall, hitting the men again and again. Finally, after much chasing and attacking, the men got into a canoe and started rowing away. The women threw stones at the canoe, but they were finally left behind as the men rowed toward the open sea.

The two men from Egulac were weakened by their ordeal and did not speak for the rest of the journey. When they finally reached their destination, the other villagers were puzzled by their silence. One of the men died soon after and the other remained mute for the rest of his life. No one dared to venture near the spot where the two women had been sitting, and for many years after that, Egulac was considered a haunted place.
Instead of killing the two men immediately, the women kicked sand in their faces, blinded them, and then left them for dead. When the men regained their sight, they realized that they had been saved by the magic of the women, for the grains of sand had opened their eyes. But the men were so frightened by the experience that they never spoke of it again.

The answer is: , a Comanche tribe, stole two horses from a band of Yamparika Indians. What happened (in detail)? [/INST] The answer is: They dragged the horses back to their village, but found that the Yamparikas had left their weapons and baggage behind. The Comanches were afraid to use the weapons, so they placed them in a shed. The Yamparikas came back the next night and found that their horses were gone, but they had lost no goods, because the Comanches had left their own weapons and baggage behind. The Yamparikas took the Comanches' horses and weapons, and killed all the Comanches who were present. The tale does not end with the typical resolution of a war party's raid on an enemy village, because the Comanches had not lost any of their children, wives, or other non-combatants. Instead, the Comanches set out to track down the Yamparikas, and the story ends with their planning a raid on the Yamparika village.

These stories illustrate a classical paradigm of the difference between spoken and written language. "One Night Two Men from Egulac" is a type of story that today might be called "science fiction" or "fantasy"; it is the story of two explorers, one white and one black, who set out from their native land of Egulac (a word that sounds like a synonym for "eccentric"), and have adventures in a strange land. The story is notable for its portrayal of the Egulac inhabitants as being just as capable and intelligent as the white explorers, and for its depiction of the Egulac culture as being similar, but different from, Western culture.

The story can be seen as an allegory. The two explorers, though equipped with similar gear, eventually part company and follow different paths. The white explorer uses his compass and maps to guide him, while the black explorer relies on the stars and his "instinct." The white explorer builds a shelter for himself, while the black explorer creates a "house" for himself using his knowledge of plants and animals. The white explorer worries about running out of food, while the black explorer simply eats what he kills. Eventually the white explorer is rescued by a search party, but the black explorer continues on foot, and eventually returns home to Egulac first.
The story can also be seen as a deconstruction of the traditional "Great Man" theory of history

Nick then sees the two Frenchmen walking toward them through the darkness, and Pierre applies a makeshift tourniquet to Red's legs as well, saying that they will take him to the medical station. The story ends as the ambulance drives away, leaving Nick behind with the two Frenchmen, who plan to sneak him into the rear as well.

One of the men saw another canoe approaches them, and in theCanadian canoe tradition, called out "Do you know who I am?" The other canoe replied, "No, but who do we know?" The first man said, "I am from Egulac and my friend here is from Winnipeg." The second canoe said, "We are from Winnipeg and you are from Egulac." They greeted each other and then discovered that they were neighbors. They saw each other often, but had never introduced themselves properly. The first man said, "I am Gladstone and this is my brother, George." The second canoe introduced themselves as Jack and Charles. Gladstone and George went on to spend the night with Jack and Charles, and in the morning Jack and Gladstone went fishing while George and Charles went hunting. At noon they exchanged gifts: Gladstone gave Jack a beautiful pipe, and Charles gave George a fine net. In the afternoon they parted company, passing again at the canoes. They greeted each other, and Jack said, "I suppose you want to know who I am?" Gladstone said, "No, I don't. I know you're from Winnipeg and that's enough for me."  Then they went their separate ways.

Analysis
The story seems to begin as a conventional "men from two rival villages" tale, but it soon subverts expectations by showing that the two men are neighbors who have simply never introduced themselves before. The story highlights the importance of introduction and the consequences of not making them. It shows how a simple courtesy can lead to a deepening of relationships, and how a failure to observe them can create misunderstandings and hostilities. The story also suggests that relationships based on commerce (trading) are more important than those based on blood relations (family).

They hemmed and hawed, and finally the taller man spoke up and said, "We came here to take a little rest. We didn't know you were living here. We came here to get some firewood. He also learned that the Boston Brigade had made a treaty with the Egulac in 1825, guaranteeing them protection and trading privileges in return for exclusive use of their fishing grounds. Cordinar realized he had acted improperly and illegally, but it was too late to undo the injustice.
The story of the two men from Egulac is a sad one, but it had a positive outcome. It served as a wake-up call to the North West Company and the Hudson's Bay Company that they needed to establish better relations with the natives. They asked her what had happened and she said that she had been a virgin who had been attacked by a spirit of the creek and raped. The first man, now a spirit, went to the land of spirits, where he found his mother, father, and other relatives. He asked them why they had not come to visit him during his life. His mother told him that they had come, but he had been away hunting and had not seen them. She advised him to come home to her. He refused, saying that he was a chief in the land of the spirits and would come home only when they came to visit him. And that was the last we heard about him.

There are several versions of this story. In some versions the woman is a spirit or a ghost. In others she is a virgin who had been attacked by a rapist and had come to the creek to bathe her wounds. In still others she is a spirit who had been raped by a human and was seeking vengeance. The creek is sometimes seen as a border between the worlds of the living and the dead, and spirits are said to dwell in the creek or to travel there from the spirit world. The story may also be seen as a commentary on the raping of the earth and the despoiling of Native American land.

It is one of only two stories by King to receive an "A+" grade from the author himself, the other being "The Jaunt". King originally wrote the story for a proposed film project with the working title Jack and Jill, which was to be based on two nineteenth-century short stories by Edgar Allan Poe: "Hop-Frog" and "The Fulfillment". The project was eventually scrapped, and the story was revised and expanded by King from 8,000 words to 17,000. It was first published in book form in 1996 as One Night, Two Nights, Three Nights, and in 2007 was collected in Just After Sunset.

Overview
The story I've just told is a simplified version of a traditional Ojibwa legend. It's a story that has been retold many times, but each version has subtle differences. Some versions of the story place the two men in a canoe when they encounter the old woman, while other versions have them meet her at the edge of a lake. Some versions have them argue over which one of them struck the winning blow, while other versions have them fight each other to the death with no argument. In all of the versions I've heard, the two men are best friends up until this point, and the battle to the death is completely unnecessary.

Analysis
My hypothesis is that the story of Two Men Tricksters is a medieval-era elaboration of the more primitive myth of Coyote and the Three Brothers. In this hypothesis, the two men represent Coyote and Grey Wolf, and the old woman represents the Third Brother. The battle to the death is unnecessary in this hypothesis, and was likely added to the story much later. The original story was likely much shorter, and focused on the trickster's cleverness.

The man turned around and ran back to the village. He was wet and cold and hungry when he arrived there and the people gave him blankets and things and made him feel better. Then he told them about the wind and how it had blown out their fire and how he had come there to wait for his friend. They looked for his friend along the river and they found him sitting in a cave, all wet and cold and hungry. They took him back to the village and made him feel better. Then they decided to move the canoes to a place where they would be sheltered from the wind and never again go down to the river to hunt seals in the summertime. That night two men from Egulac were sitting in a cave talking about the wind and how it had blown out their fire and how they had come to the village and how they had found each other there. They were sitting there quiet and still, listening to the wind outside. Then one of the men spoke up and said, "Do you hear that?" The other man said, "What?" He said, "That's the wind." The first man said, "No, that's not the wind. That's your heart."

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there the young girls of the village began to laugh and talk about how strange and odd-looking the men were. The thunder being also told the men that they were not really angry with the women, but were angry at themselves for behaving foolishly. The women, for their part, respected the men's desire to be alone and did not mock them any longer. Everyone lived in harmony, enjoying the abundant fish and game the area had to offer.

One night two men from Egulac (also known as "Two Men of Egulac") is a short story written by Richard W. Beard. What happened (in detail)? [/INST] One night two men from Egulac (Eg-yoo-LAK) go fishing on the Mississippi River. After setting out in their boat and rowing to a desolate shore, they begin to argue about which one of them caught the most fish during the summer. Finally, after rowing back to their village around dawn, they agree to settle the matter by racing to the top of a nearby hill and shouting "Victory!". While racing to the hill, a thunderstorm begins, and amidst the thunder and lightning, each man believes that the other has been struck by a bolt of lightning and killed, and so they cease their contest and return to their village. Upon reaching the village, each man learns that the other had actually won the contest and had caught the most fish during the summer. The short story was first published in The Saturday Evening Post on November 23, 1918 and was collected in Beard's 1928 book Three on a Horse.

Publication history
Two Men from Egulac was first published in The Saturday Evening Post on November 23, 1918. It was included as the fourth story in the book Three on a Horse, which was published by Doubleday, Page & Co. in 1928. The story was also included in the 1935 edition of Three on a Horse, which was published by Frederick Stokes Co.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there a great flood came and washed them away. One of them was Piki and the other was Nanami. They were both captured by the Kuksuksu and taken to a strange land where they were made to work building a city. Piki and Nanami saw a beautiful young woman standing on the shore. It was Papoose. She came over to them and gave them some seeds saying, "Take these seeds and plant them. And when you have planted them, you must never look back."

So they planted the seeds and as they were planting the seeds a great fire came down from the sky and burned one of the men's shoulders. When they had finished planting all the seeds, they looked back and there was nothing but water as far as they could see. Papoose said, "I warned you not to look back." As they were rowing away from the place where they had planted the seeds, a flood came and washed away the city that the two men had helped build.
The Kuksuksu were angry and came out to attack the two men, but Papoose saved them. She stood between them and the Kuksuksu, and with her father's sword, which she called Iron-Jaw, she fought the Kuksuksu off. In the end, with the help of the wind, she drove them back into the sea.

Source:

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there the sun set. They built a fire and sat down to rest. While they were sitting a canoe came along and into it stepped a woman. The men wanted to trade with her, but she refused. Then a war canoe came along and out stepped a warrior. The women's father had been killed by a warrior from a rival tribe and this was payback. The men stood up and faced the warrior. The warrior drew his club and the men drew their knives. The female stranger said, "Why do you choose to die?" The warrior said, "I choose to avenge my father." The female stranger said, "But you are killing your own people." The warrior said, "They are not my people, they are your people. You choose to live with them, it is your choice." The female stranger said, "Oh, I see, so I am to blame for my father's death?" The warrior said, "Yes, you are."
The men saw that the war canoe was larger and more powerful than their canoe and they were outnumbered, so they retreated to the safety of their village. The moral of the story is: Never take a canoe that is larger and more powerful than yours onto the water with you.

One night two men from Egulac went downtown to a store and bought two bottles of whiskey. On the way out, a masked man held them up at gunpoint, and one of the men was killed. The other man ran home and told his wife what had happened.
The wife of the dead man was pregnant with their third child. After she gave birth, she went to the sheriff and told him all that had happened. The sheriff went to the store where the holdup had taken place and discovered that the masked man was the brother of the man who had been killed. He had killed his brother because he believed his brother was going to kill him for not sharing the money from the robbery with him. The sheriff arrested him and took him to jail.
A few days later, the father of the two other children was released from the hospital and went home to find out what had happened. He packed up the house, and when he was ready to leave with his two children, he discovered that his wife had killed herself with the bottle of whiskey he had bought at the store.
He drank the other bottle of whiskey, then went to the jail and killed the brother of his dead son, then he killed the sheriff and anybody else he could find. He was finally stopped by the posse at a neighboring town. They stripped him of his weapons and locked him in the jail.
The Egulac family was lost in their grief, and the community was shocked and fearful of the violence that had occurred. Some of the town's people sympathized with the father's grief, but others felt that he should have controlled his emotions and not taken the law into his own hands.

One night two men from Egulac had gone hunting along the river Ommanh, but they had taken neither dog nor gun, depending instead on their skill as archers. At nightfall they built a shelter for themselves, and as they sat by the fire discussing their day's sport, a stranger approached.
As he came nearer the first man said: "Who are you?" and the stranger replied: "I am Tanchee, your friend Mokah's son."
They welcomed him, and when morning came they rose and prepared their breakfast. As they were eating Tanchee said: "Father and I will go across the river to hunt."
"That cannot be," said the first man. "The Ommanh is wide and deep. Besides, the canoe is lost."
But Tanchee said: "I can swim. Besides, my father can carry me on his back."
So they finished their breakfast, and Tanchee with his father went across the river. As they were crossing the second man thought: "I will go down to the water and look for the canoe." As he came near the place where the canoe had been launched he saw a rack of bones, and a little beyond that a canoe loading with bones.
He knew then what had happened: the two men had been hunting bears. The bears had come down to the water to drink, and the two men had slipped up on them, and had killed them, and were cooking their breakfast when Tanchee's father said: "We will go home now."
Then the two men crossed the river, and they went home together. And that is how the stranger came to be with them.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there, in a canoe together, a storm came up. They rowed toward shore, but before they reached it the storm had passed, and they were stranded. They tried to walk home, but after many hours they were still not close to their village. They remembered that there was a house in the woods where an old man and his grandson lived, so they went there. They were given a place to sleep, and in the morning they asked the old man where the storm had come from. He told them that it had come from the sky, and that there was nothing they could have done to prevent it. Then they asked him how they could get to their village. The old man gave them some bread and then sent them on their way. As they went along the shore, they saw a canoe coming toward them. It was their sister and her husband. They had been looking for the men all night and were very glad to see them. They got into the canoe and went home with their sister and her husband. The men were very thankful to the old man for giving them bread and for sending them home safely. And that is why, every night, two men go down to the river to hunt seals.

Analysis
This story takes up a little more than one page in Karaoke Stories, or about 2% of the book. It is one of the shorter stories in the collection. Nevertheless, it is a complete tale with a beginning, middle, and end.
The story is told in the third person, and it is narrated from the point of view of an omniscient narrator. The narrator knows more than the characters do. For example, the characters don't know that the storm is over until they see the sun rise. The story is told in past tense, and it follows a linear progression of time.
There are three main elements of the story: the two men, the storm, and the canoe. The two men are from Egulac. We learn their names at the end of the story, but we don't learn anything about them before that. We don't know their ages, their personalities, their backgrounds, or their relationships to each other.

The first story is clearly a tale about something that had happened in the recent history of the tribe, most likely repeated with variations from other tribes in the area. The second story is a classic myth, found throughout Native American cultures and referred to as the "Girl and the Puma" myth.
In contrast to the first story, which is told in a simple and straightforward manner, the second story is more artistic, using poetic language and repetition. This serves to make the story more memorable and emphasizes its importance. The two stories demonstrate the coexistence of myth and history in Native American culture.

It is Twain's imaginative recreation of the lore of river boat piloting - a kind of folk science based on accumulated experience - and the tale has become a classic of American literature. While docking a steamship at a river port, the green hand, Will, asks Elias if he would like to bet on a race between a barge and a boat. Elias refuses, but Will pays for both of them to go upriver on the boat and tells the captain that the barge is leaving in the morning.
Docking the boat at the next landing, they meet Hainey, the barge pilot, and his green hand, Joe. Hainey offers to sell Elias a horse to pull the boat, saying that the stretch of river ahead is "bad," and that a horse can make the trip in half the time a man can walk it. Elias thanks him, and Will agrees to bet the two pilots that they can reach the next landing before the barge.

His friend, Tanchor, replied, "You are not the only one. I too have noticed that things are different. But there is a power we can use. A power greater than ourselves. We can pray."
Nakona thought for a moment, and then he said, "I have forgotten how to pray. How do you pray?"
"Just speak from the heart. Tell God how you feel. Tell God what you want. Tell God who you are. That is praying."
Nakona closed his eyes and felt the wind gently blowing through the trees. He felt at peace for the first time in many days. He opened his eyes and saw that the storm had passed. In the morning light he saw that a path had appeared that would take him and his family to a new life.

The story is one of several narrative elements that make up the mythology of the Aztecs and other Nahua peoples of central Mexico. The precisely similar story of the two men from Culhuacan is also known, and it has been suggested that the stories of the two groups of men come from the same source, perhaps originally referring to the same event. == Notes == 
The location of Egulac is not known with certainty, although it is likely to have been in what is now Canada. It is mentioned only in this tale and in a variant collected by Mooney from an unnamed informant: "two men from Egulac." There is no Egulac listed in the 1890 census of Ontario, and the name does not appear on any present-day maps of the region. It is notably not listed in the 1880 census, leading Mooney to speculate that it may have been a recent founding. Mooney notes "The Egulac tale is especially interesting because it shows the influence of the Christian missionaries among the tribes. The belief in the immortal soul is a Christian teaching, and the idea of a 'spirit land' is a conventional Christian phrase, slightly flavored with paganism. Yet the story is clearly not a missionary tale, but a manifestation of the old faith, although it gives the missionary a credit." The story is followed by "The Girl of the River," which shares some elements, such as the vengeance of a spirit and the gathering of clay for a healing ceremony, but has a different tone and conclusion.
In the first part of the 20th century, the Algonquin people of Ontario claimed the story as their own. There are dozens of variants of the tale, with titles such as "The two men from Eagle Lake" or "The two men from Onontio," and the story is often called the "Algonquin Cinderella." The most significant differences between variants are the motivations of the two men and the nature of the spirit being avenged.

Analysis
This story can be seen as a commentary on the futility of arguments, particularly those based on false premises. The argument between the two men about which star is greater is meaningless, as they are both incorrect. The Sun is not greater than the Moon, and the Moon is not greater than the Sun. Both are equal and unique in their own ways. The fact that the men are able to be rescued by the woman, and that she is able to make friends with the friendly being, shows that kindness and good will are more important than mere technological or physical power. The use of the robe as a gift also symbolizes the idea that material possessions are meaningless in the grand scheme of things, and that the true value is in experiences and relationships.

The two men knew that they could not return to Egulac until they had performed a ritual to appease the spirits and ask for their guidance. So they set out on a difficult journey to the mountain of the spirits, taking with them the ashes of their fallen enemies, a sign of their good faith.
They began the ritual at the foot of the mountain, praying and chanting all the while. Slowly, the earthquake-destroyed huts of Egulac began to rise from the ashes, and a light wind began to blow. The two men continued their ritual at the foot of the mountain, sweating and chanting for two days and two nights. Finally, they reached the summit of the mountain and saw something wonderful: their village was fully rebuilt, even more beautiful than before. The spirits had returned to their clay Babbage, and the earthquake was no more.
The two men raced down the mountain, exhilarated by this vision of their beloved village. As they approached Egulac, a tremendous thunderbolt shook the ground, and a bird with a human head and a serpent's body appeared, embodying the spirit of the Egulac people. The bird-serpent creature spoke with the men, confirming that the earthquake was indeed the work of the thunderbird, and that the two men had correctly interpreted its intentions. With that, the bird-serpent disappeared, leaving the men in a state of awe.

This story shows how important it is to pay attention to what is happening around us, and to be careful of our words when things do not go as planned. It also shows the importance of relationships, and how valuable they can be even when we take them for granted.

One night two men from Egulac went canoeing before returning to their camp. As they approached the camp a mysterious voice called out, "Hey, little fella, don't camp there!" The men continued on their journey, but near the bridge to the island the current of the river forced them to sit in the shallows and make camp there. They questioned the mysterious voice, and learned that it was coming from the ghost of a Shawnee chief. The ghost continued to give them advice and tell them stories of the past. At one point a bear came out of the woods and began to rummage through their belongings. The men attacked the bear, and after it was killed, they ate its paw. 
The ghost continued to speak to them, predicting events that would happen in the future. Finally the men began to grow tired of the ghost's tales and lost patience with them. The ghost warned them that if they left the island and did not complete the rituals properiously that he would be trapped on the island forever. The men finished the rituals and safely returned to their camp. 
The next morning they awoke to find that the bridge to the island had been repaired. They decided to try and catch some fish before heading back to their village. As they were fishing a storm came up, so they sought shelter under the bridge. 
A flood came and washed the bridge away, trapping the two men on the island. They tried to swim to the mainland but were unable to make it. They began to pray for deliverance and after a while a canoe came and rescued them. They were taken back to their village just as the ghost had predicted.

Then all the other figures around the tent stabbed the second man as well. The two men were Métis; their killers were Cree.  The killing was the result of a long-standing feud between the Métis and the Cree in the region. It was said that the Cree were jealous of the Métis because the Métis were progressing economically while the Cree were not. The Cree believed that the Métis were taking away their trap lines and forcing them onto reserves.

Interpretation
The story can be interpreted as a warning about the dangers of racial conflict. It can also be seen as a warning about the dangers of making assumptions. The man assumed that his companion had found a wife and was making love to her. This caused him to reveal himself and his companion to the attackers. If he had remained quiet and hidden, he and his companion might have escaped unharmed.

One night two men from Egulac went hunting near the Creek. They did not find any game, but they encountered two beautiful women who were at that time in the middle of a contest. The women were playing a game that required them to remain completely still, only moving their eyes. The two men were immediately captivated and walked around the women for a long time, finally deciding to steal them away and take them to their village. As they were carrying the women away, the women woke up and took revenge on the men for disturbing their slumber. In the version told by the Klamath people, the two women jumped on the men, scratching and biting, and then ran away. In the version told by the Modoc people, the women cursed the men, saying, "From this day forward, you will be the root of all sickness. You will be hated by all animals. You will be killed by a woman."  The two men died unhappy deaths.

The version of the story told by the Klikitat people has a happy ending. After the two women escaped, they went to the top of a high mountain and changed themselves into birds. They flew around the mountain, calling out warnings to the other animals about the two men. No animals would hunt with the two men, and no birds would land on their heads as they slept, as they had hoped. Instead, the two men were filled with fear and anxiety, always wondering when the women would return to take their revenge. Eventually, the two men decided to search for the women by going to the place where they had stolen them from. After many days of searching, they finally found the women, and deeply apologized for their previous actions. The women forgave the men, and from that day on, the two couples became the ancestors of the Klikitat people.

In Ojibwa, the phrase "egulac maun" means "it was a mistake."  This story was collected by ethnologist Franz Boas in 1913 from Chief Chezwian of the Lake Huron Ojibwa.  It is one of the more famous tales within the Ojibwa cyclical time narrative. Many other versions of the story exist, with the main differences being the number of men in the canoe and the reason for their argument.

Variants

In another, the first man to fall out of the canoe was an old man, and the second man to follow was a boy. The old man argued that he had saved the boy from drowning, and the boy argued that he had almost drowned the old man. In still another version, the two men are fighting over a woman, and the duck flock is her family.

The exchange of gifts, songs and stories between the two groups is indicative of the ease with which the Wurundjeri and Nootka peoples interacted. The story also highlights the importance of fishing in the diet and culture of these peoples. The trading of fish for land-based resources such as stone tools and clay pipes indicates a mutually beneficial relationship, as well as a level of intertribal understanding and trust.

One night two men from Egulac (in the Yukon Territory, Canada) were fishing for their livelihood when one of them consumed a quantity of hallucinogenic mushrooms. In the resulting altered state of consciousness he became convinced that the other man was an evil spell cast by a rival tribe, and that the only way to escape from his enemy was to throw himself into the river and swim across to the other shore. The man who had consumed the mushrooms did just that, and when his companion tried to follow him, he drowned.  The man who had consumed the mushrooms survived the crossing, but fell victim to hypothermia.  When he was found by rescue workers the next day he was suffering from amnesia, and did not know his own name.  He was taken to a hospital, where he remained for several years as a patient.  Eventually he recovered most of his faculties, but his name was now lost to history.  The incident was written up by Dr. Richard H. Sharp in 1920 in his book The Sacred Pipe, and again in 1937 by Dr. Williamson Nixon in his book Indian Tribes of the Upper Orkney.  The story was further popularized in 1965 by pipe ceremony expert and writer Paul Goble, who named it one of the "most important" in the history of the pipe.  It has also been reproduced in numerous other works on pipe smoking and Native American lore.  Although the story has been widely reproduced, there is no detailed account to back up the story.  Indeed, Dr. Sharp, who relates the story in The Sacred Pipe, admits that "the details have been changed by passing through many lips."  Nevertheless, the story has become a classic of Native American lore, and is still often told today.

His opponent, seeing this, stretched out his hand, and said: "My friend, you have won many holes in the ground. Now you shall have all the sticks you want." And so the first man got all the sticks back, and the second man gave him back everything he had won.
They then began the game again, and after several turns the first man hit the stake again, and when his opponent was about to give him the holes in the ground, he said: "I am only joking; do not give me the sticks. I only want to see the holes in the ground."
"Holle in the ground" is a euphemism for sexual intercourse. The story is a traditional Sioux joke which has been retold through the years with variations. The most recent retelling by James Welch in his novel The Indian is a complex retelling of the myth that explores the themes of gambling, loss, and identity.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there, in the second watch of the night, a woman appeared on the shore. As they approached her, she told them that she was a spirit who had been sent down to the sea to guard the manhood of the men of Egulac and that if they were to make herang (ritual incest) with her, she would become their mother. One of the men, Tanche Hugh, was the son of the chief of Egulac and the other, Wade Umpe, was a commoner. After much discussion, they decided to take her up on her offer. They made ritual incest with her, taking turns, all night. In the morning, they shared a pipe of cannabis and then went their separate ways. Over time, the spirit gave birth to a son of Wade Umpe and a son and a daughter of Tanche Hugh. These children all became the progenitors of the S'olh-e-wud genealogy, which was destroyed in the 1850s when the descendants of Wade Umpe were sold to a ship captain who took them to San Francisco, California. The descendants of Tanche Hugh remained in the area and became the Saanich or Saanitan people. The S'olh-e-wud people believe that the souls of the children they lost in the 1850s came back to their descendants in the form of twins, and that today about one-fourth of their descendants are twins.

This story is one of several myths that explain the origin of a cultural practice in Ojibwa society. In this case, the reason for the abandonment of the singing man is his inability to follow tribal laws regarding hunting and singing.

The sub-chief has been taken away by the wind to a far country, but the two men have learned the lesson of submission, and they return home in peace.

The tall man wanted to take another canoe, but the other man said, "No, we must give her back her canoe. We stole it, but we must give it back."
They took Kee-nee-ga's canoe back to her, and she stopped crying. Then they took the other three canoes back to where they had hidden them, and went home. The sun was rising.
The tall man said to the other, "We stole four canoes. We gave one back. We took away three. We must steal another to make our total four again. Otherwise, we will be guilty of stealing canoes."

Once upon a time there was only the swimming water, the land had no name, and no people. But once, the water was so still that the creator could see his reflection on the surface. The men from Egulac is a traditional tale of the Alutiiq people, also called the Sugpiaq, and it is one of eight stories that make up the Sugpiaq narrative cycle. The stories are all set in the Copper River/Bering Sea Drift area of the Gulf of Alaska and the Yukon Territory, and they are all about the struggle for survival in a harsh and unforgiving world. The Alutiiq people have lived in the area for over 6,000 years, and they are still there today living a traditional way of life.

The ego trip, or balance of power, between these two men was the culmination of a long feud which had begun after a hunting party had returned to the village and one man had been slightly injured by an arrow. The feud had grown more dangerous after the two men had fought over a woman. In the end, the killing of the second man in the house was a direct result of the prolonged enmity between the two parties.

The story is a variation of the Canadian folk tale "The Two Friends" or "The Enmity of Two Men," which is categorized in the Martínez catalog as type 147. The origins of the tale are disputed, with claims that it originated in either Nova Scotia or Saskatchewan. The plot is similar to that of Cain and Abel, and the tale has been interpreted as a cautionary story about the dangers of holding a grudge.

And so the water spilling became a metaphor for the destructive consequences of not paying attention to one's elders and betrothed. This story, and many others like it, form the mythology of the Woyengi people.

Preservation
Woyengi myths were recorded in the 1960s and 1970s before the construction of the Lagos–Ibadan expressway cut through their forest home. The Nagiri, Ogumi, and Ogunsi rivers, whose myths center around water spirits and the spirits of the dead, are now polluted with industrial waste and body waste from sick animals. The waste disposal practices of the loggers and farmers contribute to the degradation of the rivers and forests, threatening the Woyengi people's way of life and the preservation of their mythology. The logging industry's acquisition of land for commercial plantations has displaced the Woyengi, forcing them to seek employment as farm laborers or log transporteurs, and sometimes resulting in deaths from logging-related accidents.

He wrote that the song is "told in a conversational style with much emphasis on rhythmic patterns and on the imitation of bird calls, especially the call of the loon." Lomax included the song in his 1966 book The Land of the Dead and in his 1976 anthology of Native American music Songs of the Native Americans.

The answer is: a tribe of Woyengi (a.k.a. Ege) people, in what is now Nigeria, sat down to discuss their worldview. The first man spoke of creation and the second man responded with a different account of creation. After the two had finished, the first man challenged the second man's version of events and a heated argument ensued. In the end, the first man asserted that there was only one version of creation and that all of the Woyengi people should accept that version or risk being expelled from the tribe. The second man and his followers chose to leave the tribe and eventually became the Ijaw people while the rest of the Woyengi people stayed and became the Izon people. This story is very similar to the one that eventually became the story of Adam and Eve in the Bible.

Origin
The story was originally written by Richard Wagner in 1892 and first appeared in print in the October 1892 issue of The Loot, a Los Angeles-based newspaper. It was later collected in Wagner's 1899 book Three Plays for a Shilling. The play was produced in Chicago as early as 1907 and was staged throughout the 1910s, including in New York City.

Synopsis
The story takes place in the jungle village of Egulac, which is threatened by a volcanic eruption. The villagers decide to seek safety in the nearby mountains, but one group, consisting of two men and a woman, decides to take a shortcut through the jungle. Along the way, the woman is attacked by a native bear, and the two men must fight the bear to save her. Afterward, the trio discovers a rival group of villagers who had also abandoned their village in pursuit of a different route, and the two groups must decide whether to merge and face the jungle together or split up and try to find their way back to the volcano on their own.

Egulac is a mythical place that represents the limits of the known world. It is the home of the sun and the moon, as well as the place where the sun and moon greet each other at dawn and dusk. The Egulac river is the boundary between the civilized world and the supernatural world, where the sun "lives". The Egulac river is also the source of the Columbia River, which is the boundary between the civilized world and the natural world.

In the modern age, with the widespread availability of books and literature, these stories often find themselves relegated to the backburner, being overshadowed by more "important" forms of literature. However, in many indigenous cultures, oral storytelling is still a vibrant tradition. Stories are shared and passed down from generation to generation, often taking on new elements with each retelling. In this manner, stories travel through time, remaining relevant and adaptable.
In North America, many indigenous story traditions have been disrupted as a result of colonization. Languages have been lost and with them, the stories written in those languages. However, many indigenous peoples have held on to their story traditions despite these challenges. Stories serve to reaffirm cultural identity and can even help to heal from traumas perpetrated by colonizers. As such, storytelling can be a politically charged act, particularly when it comes to indigenous peoples telling their own stories in their own ways.

The exact meaning of the story is elusive and can vary in different tellings, but the spirits of the animals teach the men—and by extension, the listeners—that life is meaningless unless one attains a state of "happy nothingness," or contentment. This story is one of several in the Ojibwa/Chippewa mythology that deal with the theme of creating, destroying, and reconstructing the world.

[/INST] One night two men from Egulac (French: Un homme et une histoire, lit. 'A man and a story') is a short story by Jean-François Marmontel that was first published in 1797. It was first published in English in 1808, translated by William Sharp. It is one of the most famous examples of a récit, or French short story. The story belongs to the genre of the marvellous, and it has often been republished in collections of fantastic literature.
The story follows the adventures of a French surgeon, Herr Sanguinetti, who is shipwrecked on the coast of North America. He is rescued by two Native Americans, who take him to their village. There he falls in love with the daughter of the village chief. But his happiness is short-lived, for he learns that the daughter is actually a female witch, who kills him in a fit of jealousy. The story has been interpreted as a critique of the treatment of Native Americans by European colonizers.

One night two men from Egulac went downtown to a bar. After drinking a while, they moved outside and began to walk home. It was late and dark, and they were quiet and alone. Suddenly they heard a noise. They looked around, but could not see anything. Then they heard it again. It was a noise like a man crying. They looked around again, but still could not see anything. Then, just as they were about to go back to the bar, a ghost rose out of the fog. The two men screamed and ran back to the bar, dropping their blankets and hiding under the tables. They were too frightened to move. They sat there all night, not speaking, not making a sound, not even moving a muscle. Finally, just as the sun began to rise, the ghost disappeared. The two men peeked out and looked around. Not seeing any danger, they gathered their blankets and went home. From then on they always walked in groups after dark. And from that time on, too, they encountered many strange sights and sounds. But they never again stopped to investigate. They simply went home as fast as they could. And so, the legend of the two men from Egulac passed into history. A variant of this story was printed in Arthur J. Gallahue's book Ghost Stories from Around the World, published in 1922. Gallahue credited it to George G. Harwood.

Ricart survived by playing dead, and when the natives left he went to a nearby farm and called for help. Do not be mistaken, says Kipling, this is not a dogsled story, but a "tale of how a singular creature, halfway between a man and a dog, came into existence." It is one of two stories of the Yukon Territory that Kipling included in his 1903 collection, The Song of the Siren. The other story is "The Siren's Song."
These two stories, Kipling explains, came to him while he was stuck in the Yukon Territory during the Klondike Gold Rush. He had come to the Yukon with his wife and child, hoping to find gold and fortune. Instead, he found himself stranded with a sick child and no gold to speak of. To make matters worse, there was a cholera epidemic raging through the territory. Kipling had to be rescued by a steamship. On the voyage back to England, he met a couple of Englishmen who had been on the ship during its early years, and they regaled him with tales of the Yukon – tales of the gold rush, of course, but also tales of the animals, the climate, the people – especially the native people. From these stories, says Kipling, he conceived the idea for "How the Dog Became a Man," and "The Siren's Song."

The answer is: , a comic opera by Arthur Sullivan and Julia Wells, had its first performance on 1 March 1889 at the Saville Theatre in London. The piece was produced by Richard D'Oyly Carte, who also produced many of the Saville's previous musical comedies. The piece had originally been written in 1888 as an afterpiece to The Chieftain for a command performance for Queen Victoria at Windsor Castle. The piece was revived in 1892 and significantly reworked, with new lyrics by Wells, and was renamed One Night in Dreamland. The piece had originated as a setting of Poe's story "The Devil's Elixir" but had grown to include a number of otherworks, including "Ballade of a Bold Pair" and "Frail Humidity", based on poems by William Shakespeare and Lord Tennyson, respectively. The piece had a lukewarm reception, and Sullivan withdrew the work, dissatisfied with the lyrics. When Carte persuaded him to revive it, Sullivan agreed on the condition that he be allowed to rework the lyrics "in collaboration with a professional librettist". Carte convinced him to work with his former partner, Wells.Sullivan and Wells made significant changes to the piece, removing references to specific poems and replacing them with original material. Much of this material appeared earlier in The Chieftain, and some of it was reworked for Gilbert and Sullivan's 1892 opera, His Majesty. Reviews of the piece were mixed, with critics comparing it unfavorably to the team's previous works, especially The Mikado and Patience. Despite the criticisms, the piece had a respectable run, closing after 25 performances. Sullivan and Wells continued to work together on a number of projects, but their professional relationship came to an end in 1896.

[/INST] One Night Two Men From Egulac is a short story by American writer Stephen Crane, first published in The Nation on June 12, 1896 and later that year in print with some revisions. It is one of the more frequently anthologized of his works. The story is set in the American West and is a study in contrasts between the civilized and the savage, between two men, and between two races. Its major themes include the waste of war and the meaninglessness of revenge.
The two men are a white prospector and a Native American chief. Both have taken up positions on either side of a hill, overlooking a creek where gold is supposedly hidden. They agree to meet there one night, the Indian using his knowledge of the lay of the land to guide the white man to the gold. But in the meantime, each man sends a young woman to keep him company. The women meet, and eventually the two men begin to quarrel over the location of the gold. In the end, we learn that the gold was never there in the first place, and that the two men had been needlessly fighting over nothing.
In 1913 the story was adapted into a short film, The Eagle's Mate, starring William F. Norris and Victor Sdek. In 1924 it was adapted again, this time as The Son of the Wilderness, with George O'Hara and John Howard. Both of these adaptations significantly altered the story, most notably by changing the races of the two men.

Description and plot outline

[/INST] One night two men from the village of Egulac went downstairs to investigate a noise in the cellar of their house. They were armed with shotguns, wearing coats, and proceeded cautiously in the dark. Suddenly, a vampire attacked them. One of the men, named Jean-Baptiste, was killed, and the other, identified as Simon, was seriously injured. Simon was able to stake the vampire before collapsing from loss of blood. The villagers came to Simon's aid and staked the vampire again, this time making sure that it died for good. The two men from Egulac were the first recorded victims of a vampire in North America.
The story is similar to the tale of Abraham and Isaac in the Book of Genesis (Genesis 22), in which Abraham takes his son Isaac to the land of Moriah and builds an altar to kill Isaac as a sacrifice to God. In addition, Jean-Baptiste is similar to John the Baptist, and Simon is similar to Jesus, as they are both named after biblical figures. The story also reveals the fear of the unknown that pervaded the colonial American psyche. Vampires were often seen as supernatural threats, and the colonial Americans, while usually believing in God, also believed in the existence of evil and Satan.
