There was another version of the myth that explained the motive behind the expedition. In this version, the Egulac men had stolen a canoe belonging to the Onondagas and were paddling it through the fog when they were attacked. They had lost their way and were fighting their way back to their own village when they were captured and brought back to Onondaga.
In either case, the upshot was that the Egulac men were taken prisoners to Onondaga and eventually returned home again, much to the relief of their families, who had been grieving for them. The war-party returned to Onondaga, where the captives were handed over to the women, who painted the men's faces and clamped sticks upon their noses and lips, and pierced their ears.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. As they swam along the shore, they saw a canoe with five bags of presents floating toward them. They dropped their own canoe and swam to the canoe with the presents, which was made of a mysterious, unusual wood, and opened the canoe. They found nothing but dry sticks and clay pots filled with sand. They were angry and began to load the canoe onto their own canoe, but as they were doing so, four more canoes with presents floated toward them. They welcomed the givers of the presents, who turned out to be members of a tribe from upriver. The two men had never seen people with such dark skin before. The leaders of the upriver tribe wanted to trade gifts with the two men, but the two men said they had nothing to offer in return. The upriver tribe then gave the two men a boat and some clay pots, and told them to come upriver to their village for a festival in their honor. On the journey to the upriver village, the two men saw many other canoes with presents, all bound for the same village. When the two men arrived at the village, they were decorated with clay paint and feathers, and they danced all night long. In the morning, the two men returned home, feeling happy and wealthy.

After they had gathered all the pieces they got up to leave and the earth opened up under their feet and swallowed them both up.

One night two men from Egulac (in the Yukon territory) were arguing over who was the stronger. They began to fight, and soon all the other men in the village had gathered around them, laughing and betting on the outcome. The two fighters were soon exhausted, and with the crowd shouting for a decision, one of the men picked up a bone and threw it at his opponent. His aim was so good that it broke the other man's arm.
The crowd roared for the victor, but he took a solemn oath never again to lift a hand against another human being. The other man was taken to a doctor, and while he was healing the doctor discovered that his patient had lost the use of his other arm many years ago.
The two men, upon learning this, became the best of friends and went about their lives, no longer caring who was the stronger. The Yukoners remembered this event for many years, and it became a powerful lesson about the foolishness of violence.

The Wendigo is a flesh-eating demon of the forest. It has the head of a bear, the body of a man, and the legs of a deer. It steals the bodies of its victims, leaving their spirits to wander the forest aimlessly. The Wendigo is not a creator god, but a god of transformation. It is best known for its ability to turn humans into Wendigo.
In the myths of many Native American tribes, the Wendigo takes the form of a human being or animal, but is recognized by its eyes, which are described as glowing or fiery. Wendigo myths are relatively uniform across the Algonquin-speaking tribes of the northeast, but each tribe's version of the myth is slightly different.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there a great thunderstorm came up. The two men were blown in different directions, and when they came back together they could not find each other in the darkness. One of the men had a good coat but no matches, and the other had matches but no coat. They searched for each other calling back and forth, and after more than an hour they met again at the place where they had started. By that time they were both wet and cold. They warmed themselves near a fire made from driftwood, and after they had warmed themselves they went back to their village. And that night two men from Egulac slept together.

There are many versions of this story. In some the men are hunting seals on the ice when the storm comes up. In others they are fishing in a canoe when the wind and rain begin. In still others they are playing rugby, or playing cards, or just sitting in their cabin staring at the rain. But the essential element in all of them is the separation of the two men in the darkness and their subsequent reunion after they have lost all sense of direction. And in none of them do the men have a coat and matches at the same time.
The version I have given is the one told by a Tlingit Eskimo of the Pacific Northwest. In some other versions the men are named, and in some they talk to each other all night. But in no version do they talk about the weather. They just happen to be caught in it. And in no version is there any suggestion that the men are queer.
This story is not about seals. It's about how the weather can separate us from our fellows and make us lose our direction and our sense of identity, and how important it is to have a friend, even if you don't have a name.

One night two men from Egulac went out to hunt, equipped with their bows and arrows. As they separated to hunt individually, the heavens became a scene of amazing beauty and wonder: the stars came closer together and seemed to dance around the moon, which had grown larger and more beautiful than either of the men had ever seen. They marveled at the sight, and then returned home to their village. From then on, every night one of the men would go out to hunt while the other stayed behind to see what would happen to the moon. The Egulac men believed that the Great Spirit was making the moon grow larger and more beautiful for the benefit of their tribe.  After many nights, the hunter who had been going out alone began to notice that the moon was no longer getting larger, but was instead gradually shrinking back to its normal size. One night, as he approached his village, he saw that all the Egulac women and children had gathered outside to see the moon, which had shrunken until it was as small as an orange. The men exchanged worried glances, and then a voice came over the wind, saying: "The spirit of the moon is sad. He wants you to know that nothing can stop the world from turning, but he can make the moon bigger or smaller as he wishes."  From then on, the men of Egulac took turns making sacrifices to the moon, usually giving up a valuable possession, in the hope of making the Spirit of the Moon happy and keeping the world from turning too fast.  Over time, the people of Egulac came to believe that their sacrifices made the moon grow larger, even though in fact the moon's changes were caused by shifts in the Earth's orbit.

The hunters watched as she dropped the contents of her armfuls into the fire, one by one, letting the leaves, berries, and herbs burn and create three different colors of smoke.
The woman explained that the blue smoke was for protection, the white smoke for love, and the red smoke for war. Then she added, "Whatever you choose, make it strong. And remember, once you begin, you must finish what you started."
The hunters chose the smoke of war, and they spent the rest of their lives fighting in wars.

And it was more than wind, it was a spirit driving them back. They had not gone back to their village, they had gone out to the place where the spirit of the water lives.
They built a shelter there and made a canoe and began to hunt seals again. And after many days of this they returned to their village and told what had happened. And their friends said, "Well, maybe one of you did not know that the spirit of the water was angry and drove you back." But the two men knew that it was not that. It was that they had gone out to the place where the spirit of the water lives, and there they had taken shelter under a tree, and the tree had crashed down and knocked a hole in their canoe. And they had patched it up as best they could and resumed their hunting. And the spirit of the water was angry because they had come down to hunt seals in his house.

One night two men from Egulac (or Egulak) went hunting near a village in the forest. They stumbled upon a wolf who had been killed by a hunter from the village. One man said, "This is a bad day for that hunter. He has lost his wolf." The other man said, "It is not the wolf that is dead, but the hunter. If we were to give the hunter's name, the wolf would come back to life." They decided to steal the dead wolf's body and take it back to their village. They thought that by doing this, they could trick the hunter's ghost into returning to the scene of his death, thereby revealing his name. However, when they got back to their village and were preparing to split up the wolf's body, the ghost of the hunter appeared to them in a thunderstorm and revealed his name, causing a shock to the two men.

It has been suggested that the origin of the tale is a conflict between two hunting parties over a valuable fur, perhaps a beaver, which had been trapped and killed. One party might have killed the other party's animal and then stolen its carcass, or the two parties might have accidentally killed each other while pursuing the same animal. In some versions of the myth, the ghost of the slain hunter seeks revenge upon the survivors. The myth may also incorporate an element of the beaver conflict myth, in which the two parties feud over a sexual partner, often a married woman desireously courted by both men.The first known publication of the tale was in 1899 with "The Revenge of the Slain Hunter" by William J. Wolfe. Others have retold the tale with varying degrees of faithfulness to the original. The most notable variant is that told by Jerry Wallace and Bruce H. Williams in their book Western Folklore, which essentially reverses the roles of the two men and the hunter.

One night two men from Egulac went out to hunt deer. They had gone a short way into the forest when a bear came towards them. One of the men took his club and threw it at the bear, hitting its head. The bear fell down immediately. They both knew that it was a magical bear because of the way it had fallen down without fighting back. The two men decided to take the bear home with them. They reached Egulac around dawn. The chief and the people were beside themselves with fear and wonderment when the two men entered the village with the magical bear. The bear was put in a pit where it could be kept until it could be used for fur and meat. The next day, a celebration was held for the two hunters and for the bear. The bear had been a powerful spirit, and its spirit was released by the hunters. It was recognized that the two men had been on a quest to bring back a part of the spiritual world to their village, and they had succeeded.

The Story of the Two Men from Egulac is a symbolic narrative that describes the transition of two men from the ordinary world of their village to the supernatural world of the bear. In the beginning, the two men are ordinary hunters going about their daily business. They are in the forest, a place of transformation, when they encounter the bear, a powerful spirit. The bear represents the spiritual world, and the hunters, who have always known that the forest is a place of magic, are able to recognize the spiritual power of the bear. They do not kill the bear for food or for its fur, but they take it home with them because they know that they are dealing with a spiritual being. The bear's spirit is released, but not before it has been honored with a celebration in its honor.

Background
The Cree people have a rich oral tradition of storytelling. Their creation legends are full of mythical beings and events. Many of these stories have been written down, but the meanings are often quite different from those found in Western literature. For the Cree people, these stories are an intricate web of meaning that must be experienced on a sensory level. The stories are not just tales to be understood intellectually, but must be felt in the same way that one might feel the wind or the sun.

Origins
"One Night Two Men from Egulac" is based on the true story of two 19th century Canadian farmers who drowned while fishing on the Ottawa River. The farmers were William Clark and Edward Stanley, who set out in a double canoe to fish for bass on May 24, 1855. They got into trouble when they capsized their canoe in the rapids near the village of Clarence Creek (now Clarence-Rockland). Their bodies were found the next day by a steamboat passenger who was familiar with the rapids. He guided the steamboat's pilot around the dangerous currents where the two men had capsized their canoe.
Passed down through word of mouth, the song was first recorded in 1957 in Ottawa by singer-songwriter Spider Web Smith. Smith learned the song from his friend Don Chivers, who heard it from his grandfather, who was a lighthouse keeper on the St. Lawrence River. Mary seems to prefer Dunstan, who is more successful and wealthy than Hennessey. Hennessey thinks that his only recourse is to murder Dunstan and claim that an Indian attacked them both, thus eliminating his rival and winning the approval of Mary's family. He deliberately misses Dunstan during a buffalo hunt, letting the rifle barrel swing wide, and faked an Indian attack on themselves. Dunstan is seriously injured and cannot fight back. Ekalak remembered his maternal uncle Hadushkuy, who had told him that if anyone jumped on his head he should push his hands down the back of his neck. So he pushed Harduskuy's hands down the back of his neck and pulled his arms up over his head. In this position Egush could not move, and Ekalak began to ride him like a horse. Egush struggled for a long time, eventually toppling Ekalak off him and running away in the dark. In the morning they found Ekalak lying on the ground where they had swum. They lifted him up and rubbed his back, which hurt him a great deal. Then they went home to breakfast. After breakfast Ekalak said to Egush, "Last night you rode me like a horse. Why did you do that?" "Because you pushed my head down," said Egush. "Well, when I pushed your head down I was pushing your skull. You have a thick skull. That's why you could ride me like a horse. But I don't think you have a thick skull. I think your skull is normal. That's why I could ride you like a horse." 'Well, Maybe it was because of the rocks,' said Egush. 'Yes, maybe it was because of the rocks,' said Ekalak. Then they went outside and looked at the sun.

This is the dilemma faced by the protagonist in Booth Tarkington's 1932 Pulitzer Prize-winning novel The Best Years of Our Lives, widely considered a depression-era classic.
Like much of Tarkington's work, the novel is a period piece. Set in the 1930s, it tells the story of a formerly wealthy young man, Alonzo Tyree, who through a series of poor decisions and misfortunes finds himself penniless and seeking to re-establish his position in the world. Along the way he receives varying degrees of assistance from a number of characters, some of whom are genuinely trying to help, while others seek to take advantage of him.
Though the novel was finished in 1932, and even published in serial form in The Saturday Evening Post starting in September 1932, it did not appear in book form until 1938. This was due in part to Tarkington's meticulous revision process. Over the course of several years he thoroughly reworked the novel, adding new chapters and revising old ones. According to Tarkington, this was necessary because "the story, being a complex one, required a complex treatment." Upon its release, The Best Years of Our Lives was praised for exactly this complexity, as well as for its portrayal of the period, which one reviewer described as "the era of the banquet, the automobile, the motion picture, and all-around ease and comfort."

One version has it that the two men were arguing over a game of stickball, and in his anger the loser cursed the victor, saying, "Your game stick is a false stick. You have lost your magnetism. Be henceforth a woman." The other version has it that the two men were lovers and that one of them had left the other for a female. In both cases, the wronged man cursed the other, and out of the tension and drama of the situation, the two men were transformed into women. This myth may be partially responsible for the Cherokee perception of the number two as being inherently negative.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the lake, A duck was stuck in the piece of lake, they tried to get it out but they were too late, The Indians laughed and said "Blessed are the young strangers who try to save a duck." The next night the same two men were fishing on the lake, the duck was floating on the water, they wanted to catch it but the duck was too fast, they missed it twice, the third time they caught it, they were overjoyed, they killed the duck, they were going to eat it raw, the Indians said "Blessed are the young strangers who take their first duck."  This story is a part of a larger narrative that addresses the issue of emulation in Native American and European American relations. The story seems to say that while the Europeans (or "young strangers") may imitate the Native Americans, doing so can be detrimental. The proper way for the Europeans to approach the Native Americans is through the establishment of a relationship based on mutual respect.

== Notes == 
This story is from the Muskego storytelling tradition of the Chippewa/Ojibwa people. It was collected by Mary S. Griffin and published in her 1917 book Tell Me a Story: From the oral literature of the Chippewa Indians. The story appears again in the 1977 collection Alberta Indian Legendary Narratives, vol. 1, edited by Don Burton and Diane Braesch.
In the 1917 version, the men are not named. In the 1977 version, they are named Shikak and Kabutz. The morphed word "Egulac" is a shortened form of "Eguh-land," which is a Chippewa/Ojibwa term for the area around Lake Superior.

They were astonished and excited. They followed the path the moose took and came to a pond. On the other side they saw a lodge and smoke coming from the chimney.
They crossed the pond in their canoe and knocked on the door of the lodge. A bear came out and they knew that this was the home of the Great Bear Queen.
The queen came to the door and invited them in. She gave them fish to eat and told them tales of the stars and the moon. Then she took them outside and showed them the dip net that her husband the Great Bear had made for her.
She told them how he had made the net and where he had found the dipper handle. Then she made them a basket of corn and straw.
They started to leave, but she gave them a basket of corn and a stick of wood that had a bear claw on it. She told them that if they ever got lost in the woods to follow the path down to the pond and shake the stick. If her husband the Great Bear heard them he would come and help them.
The two men went home with full stomachs and happy hearts. They talked about the adventures they had and the wonderful things they had seen. From then on they never quarreled about who would get the shorter stick. Instead they counted their blessings and were grateful for the generosity of the Great Bear Queen and her husband the Great Bear.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. It was a full moon night. As they approached the river a wave knocked a coconut from the head of one of the men. The other man said: "Let's follow the drift of the coconut." They followed the coconut down the river and found themselves on the coast of a large island. They explored the island and found it was full of cannibals. They took a vote and decided to leave the island and return to their village. If they had stayed, they would have become the food of the cannibals. After leaving the island, they stepped onto their canoe and began to paddle back to their village. Just as they thought they were home free, a rubber tree tree fell from the canopy of the jungle and hit the other man on the head killing him. The man who survived returned to his village and warned his people about the dangers of the island and how he and his companion had nearly become the meal of the cannibals. 
The Island of Meade is a story that has been retold through oral tradition in the Philippines. It is a warning to be careful on full moon nights and not to swim alone. The story has been interpreted as a warning against male homosexuality, because the two men in the story are often assumed to be lovers. The story has also been linked to the Maltese Cross, a symbol of the Knights Templar. Some scholars believe that the story originated from a warning given to the Knights Templar about the dangers of the island, and that the two men in the story represent the Templar's seal of the Maltese Cross. The symbol is interpreted as a warning to stay away from the island of Meade, and a reminder of the dangers of male homosexuality. The story has also been compared to the legend of Zazu, a similar legend from the Mesoamerican region.

Harper is startled by a knock at his door, and he finds two strange men standing in his doorway. They identify themselves as Adam White and Noah Claypole, and they claim to be traveling salesmen. After they dry themselves off from the rain, the three men engage in conversation. It soon becomes apparent that Claypole is illiterate, and Harper realizes that White is attempting to swindle him. Harper tries to expose the scam, but Claypole beats him up and forces him to pay them for a worthless "investment" in a lumber company. The play ends with Harper sitting in his armchair, knocked down again by Claypole, as White celebrates the fooling of yet another mark.

One night two men from a village in Egulac (a village in the Upper Ottawa Valley, near the present-day Quebec-Ontario border) went fishing. They caught and were preparing to cook a wolf, when a rival group of fishermen came and disputed their catch. One of the original two men killed one of the rivals with his club, and the other rushed at the remaining rival, but accidentally killed him with his spear. Feeling that they could not stay in the village any longer, the two men left, paddling their canoe toward the west. They eventually reached the coast of Hudson Bay and lived there for several years before returning to Egulac by way of the Rideau Canal. The story is repeated with slight variations in a number of Algonquin villages. It is also told with some variations among the Ojibwa/Chippewa. This is a variant of the Wolf Story.
The man who killed the rival was known as "the man who went away." His companion was known as "the elder." These two roles areassigned in the telling of the story. The murderer often goes into hiding, and the elder may go in search of him. Sometimes the murderer comes forth and admits what he has done. In some versions of the story, the elder son of the murderer may take revenge on the rival family.
This story is part of a literary tradition that includes other tales about hunting accidents and homicides, such as "The Boy and His Dog" and "The Hatchet War." These stories have been interpreted as reflecting the transition of Algonquin society from a hunter's lifestyle to one dependent on trade and farming.

They spoke the languages of the fish, the great bear, the red man, and the corn. They took their fish home to their families, and their families ate well that night. From then on, whenever they went out in their canoe, they would speak the languages of the water, the south, the west, and the east, and they would catch fish. And that is how Naglem and Ikum learned to speak the ways of the world.

Plot
In the middle of a barren desert, two men are chased by a group of their enemy. After running for miles, they scale a mountain and seek refuge in a cave. One of the men, young and strong, climbs higher on the mountain and builds a windmill to pump water from the ground. The other man, weak and sickly, stays at the bottom of the mountain and provides shelter for himself and his companion. After many years, the weak man dies. The strong man, now an old man, climbs down from the mountain and joins the women and children of his tribe living in the desert.

It was first published in the magazine Argosy, vol. 1, no. 4, July 1927. This story is one of the more bizarre tales of the weird and is a good example of the type of story that H. P. The author, Edward W. Stanton, was a prolific writer of pulp fiction. Among his many works were stories, novels, and plays. He was also a magician and consultant for several mystery magazines. He is best known for his work as a writer for the mystery magazines The Shadow and Strange Stories. He was an active member of the National Police Gazette Club. Stanton was a founding member of the New York branch of the International Association of Mystery Writers and served as its president from 1931 to 1937. He was also a member of the Authors' Guild, the Dramatists' Guild, and the National Society of Newspaper Editors. He died in 1956 in Englewood, New Jersey.
